Article Title: A Scottish wildlife rescuer saved a starving badger cub trapped in a cattle trough, but officials denied his request to keep her; now he is fighting to retain the animal he says cannot survive in the
Article Text:
Rescued from a cattle trough in April, Harriet was nursed back to health by ecologist Graeme Wilson.

From a desperate rescue to an unusual bond

Why the ecologist wants to keep Harriet

Wildlife experts raise concerns

A chance encounter with a helpless animal has turned into a complicated battle over wildlife protection, rehabilitation and the limits of human intervention. When Scottish ecologist Graeme Wilson rescued a starving badger cub from a cattle trough, he expected to nurse her back to health. Instead, the experience left him convinced that returning her to the wild could put her life in danger. Now, he is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities.According to the BBC, Harriet was discovered in April trapped inside a cattle trough, around 100 metres from her sett in the Scottish Borders. Wilson was called to help the young animal and took responsibility for her recovery, gradually nursing her back to health.However, her behaviour soon raised concerns about whether she could survive independently. Given her bottle feeding response and familiarity with humans, Wilson suspected Harriet was hand-reared before her rescue.As reported by The Telegraph, Wilson believes the cub has become accustomed to humans to such an extent that releasing her into the countryside could expose her to serious risks. He fears she might approach people while out walking, potentially placing herself in a dangerous situation.Wilson operates GW Ecology, an independent wildlife rescue and rehabilitation service from his home in Denholm. Alongside caring for injured animals, his work involves ecological surveys to identify protected species at proposed development sites. He also organises bat walks, workshops and educational activities to encourage greater awareness of wildlife conservation.The ecologist applied to NatureScot for an educational licence that would allow him to continue caring for Harriet while helping the public understand badgers and the challenges involved in rehabilitating protected wildlife.However, the application was rejected. NatureScot suggested that Harriet should either be returned to the wild or transferred to a zoo. Wilson believes neither option would adequately address her circumstances. While a release could expose her to injury or death, he fears a conventional zoo environment would leave her isolated and distressed.The disagreement has brought wider questions about the responsibilities involved in wildlife rehabilitation into focus. The BBC reported that the British Wildlife Rehabilitation Council has stressed the specialist nature of caring for wild animals.Paul Reynolds, who chairs the organisation, has highlighted the importance of suitable facilities, species-specific care, veterinary supervision and an understanding of an animal's natural behaviour. The council also distinguishes responsible rehabilitation from keeping wild animals permanently in captivity for educational or personal purposes.According to The Telegraph, the organisation maintains that an animal becoming accustomed to human contact should not automatically be considered grounds for permanent captivity.Harriet's future remains uncertainNatureScot has indicated that discussions with Wilson and other relevant organisations are continuing in an effort to find a practical resolution. The authority has emphasised that Harriet's welfare remains central to its decision-making process. Police Scotland has also been made aware of the situation.Meanwhile, the Scottish SPCA advises people who encounter sick or injured badgers to contact its rescue officers rather than attempting to handle the animals themselves. Young cubs found away from their setts may need help, and frightened or injured badgers may attack.Wilson still wants a safe future for Harriet. Whether that means an exception to the usual rules or another arrangement, the case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.Images Courtesy: istock and BBC
Article Summary: Harriet the badger cub was rescued from a cattle trough in April. Ecologist Graeme Wilson nursed her back to health but is concerned about her future. He is fighting for permission to give Harriet a permanent home, despite opposition from wildlife authorities. The case highlights the difficult balance between individual animal welfare and the principles of wildlife conservation.

Article Title: From classroom to billion-dollar fortune: How Chinese siblings struck gold in the stock market
Article Text:
How Chinese siblings struck gold in the stock market

A stock market debut has delivered a billion-dollar glow-up for a former elementary school teacher and his sister in China, turning them into billionaires after shares of their adhesive products company skyrocketed nearly eightfold on their first day of trading.Michael Mai, 62, who once taught at an elementary school in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan, now has an estimated fortune of $2.5 billion following the listing of Crown New Materials Technology on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Tuesday.His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as the company's vice-chairperson, has also made it to the billionaire club, with an estimated net worth of $2 billion.The company, which Mai chairs and leads as CEO, made its stock market debut at 16.98 yuan per share. Its shares subsequently jumped as much as 787%, according to the Shenzhen bourse, mainland China's second-largest stock exchange. The estimated fortunes of the siblings are based on their respective stakes in the business, Forbes reported.Mai is an Australian citizen and permanent resident of Hong Kong. Crown New Materials Technology, founded in 2000, is headquartered in Zhongshan, the same city where he reportedly worked as a teacher.Crown New Materials Technology makes binding agents and other adhesive products used by major brands, including Tesla and Apple. Its products help hold together components used in a variety of retail products, ranging from vehicle roofs to semiconductors in smartphones, according to the company's website.The business has expanded its manufacturing operations to five plants, with four located across China and one in Vietnam, CNN reported.The sharp rally in the company's shares was followed by a correction on Wednesday morning, when they eased to around 77 yuan ($12) apiece. The surge on the previous day had prompted the company to issue a statement asking investors to “invest rationally.”The listing comes against the backdrop of a difficult spell for China's stock markets. Weak consumer spending and concerns about a possible bursting of the AI bubble have weighed on equities in recent months.Key Chinese indexes have fallen more than 20% from their June peaks, entering bear market territory.Beijing responded two weeks ago by injecting $19 billion into exchange-traded funds, according to Bloomberg data. This was its biggest intervention since early 2025, when US President Donald Trump's tariff offensive sent global markets into turmoil.
Article Summary: Michael Mai, 62, once taught at an elementary school in the southern Chinese city of Zhongshan. His sister, Mai Huixia, 64, who serves as the company's vice- chairperson, has an estimated net worth of $2 billion. Crown New Materials Technology makes binding agents and other adhesive products used by major brands.

Article Title: US midterm fallout: Trump's India envoy Sergio Gor may replace Marco Rubio - report
Article Text:
File photo: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US ambassador to India Sergio Gor stand for the national anthem, as they attend a Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai.

As Washington prepares to recover from the less than ideal performance of the Republican party during the midterms, reports suggest a possible overhaul in senior leadership.US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has emerged as a possible contender for senior positions in president Donald Trump's administration following the recent setbacks in the midterm elections, with his name reportedly circulating for roles including White House chief of staff and secretary of state.Gor, a former senior White House aide and close Trump ally, has been discussed within the administration as a potential candidate for a bigger role during the second half of Trump's term, according to a report by The Washington Sun, citing 10 people familiar with internal discussions. There is also growing speculation among State Department officials that Gor is interested in a promotion.Well-connected within the administration and known for his direct access to Trump, Gor has increasingly taken part in high-level diplomatic engagements, acquiring influence beyond his role as ambassador to India. He is also seen as an important link between Washington and several Asian countries, as well as a close confidant of secretary of state Marco Rubio According to the report, Gor's name has come up for several senior positions, including replacing Rubio as secretary of state or Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Some officials have also discussed the possibility of him taking over as deputy secretary of state from Chris Landau.Neither Rubio nor Wiles has indicated any intention of leaving their positions. However, speculation in Republican and State Department circles suggests Rubio could eventually leave the Cabinet to prepare for a potential presidential bid in 2028 or 2032.Wiles' position, meanwhile, is also believed to be under scrutiny within Trump's inner circle.Landau was also reportedly believed to be considering leaving after the midterms if Republicans lost control of Congress, anticipating potentially difficult congressional investigations. However, he subsequently denied having any plans to quit, telling The Sun that he had never indicated an intention to leave the State Department.Gor, however, dismissed the speculation, saying he had no interest in another position and had not discussed taking up a different role with anyone.Calling the report “complete and total b*******”, Gor praised Rubio as the most qualified and accomplished secretary of state, describing him as irreplaceable and a close friend. “I have zero interest in any other role,” he said.The State Department also rejected the claims. Assistant secretary for global public affairs Dylan Johnson said Rubio and Gor shared a strong professional relationship and personal friendship, dismissing the speculation as rumours based on anonymous sources. A White House official similarly described the report as fake, saying Gor had no interest in another position and believed Wiles and Rubio were doing a phenomenal job.Despite the denials, Gor's growing diplomatic profile has drawn attention within the administration. A Trump adviser told The Sun that the president “loves the guy”, crediting Gor with bringing deals to Trump during his years outside office rather than seeking favours from him.Since taking charge of the US embassy in New Delhi in November 2025, Gor has helped facilitate several high-level visits to India, including those by Rubio, commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and then-Army secretary Dan Driscoll. His responsibilities have also extended beyond India, with his dual role as ambassador and special envoy for South and Central Asia allowing him to participate in meetings with senior foreign officials, including Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.Rubio has visited India twice this year, and the two have travelled together frequently since Gor's appointment. They also appeared together in Atlanta at a G20 summit last week.Gor was also central to Rubio's visit to Uzbekistan last month, part of the Trump administration's efforts to deepen ties with resource-rich Central Asian countries. Born in Uzbekistan when it was part of the Soviet Union, Gor has used his background and regional connections in his additional role as special envoy for South and Central Asia.His approach to diplomacy is seen by some officials as closely aligned with Trump's emphasis on dealmaking and promoting American business interests.Gor, who worked on Trump's 2024 election campaign, has previously been linked to the business interests of the president's family. His publishing company has published Trump's books, and he is particularly close to Donald Trump Jr. Before leaving for India, Gor was sworn in as ambassador during an Oval Office ceremony at which Trump described him as a “great guy” and said he was “very proud” of him.His tenure in New Delhi has also attracted attention for his hands-on management style. According to two people familiar with the embassy's operations, Gor has exercised an unusual degree of control over personnel decisions, including pushing out career State Department employees and locally hired staff.Rubio had earlier defended Gor's appointment, telling The New York Times that his “access to the president” made him “an enormous asset” for both India and the State Department.However, whether Gor's connections would translate into a Senate-confirmed Cabinet position remains uncertain. All Senate Democrats voted against his confirmation as ambassador as part of a larger package of nominees.Before joining the Trump administration, Gor spent roughly a decade working on Capitol Hill, primarily for Republican senator Rand Paul. At the White House Office of Presidential Personnel, he was responsible for identifying and vetting candidates for thousands of political appointments across the federal government.
Article Summary: US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has emerged as a possible contender for senior positions in president Donald Trump's administration. His name reportedly circulating for roles including White House chief of staff and secretary of state. Gor dismissed the speculation, saying he had no interest in another position and had not discussed taking up a different role.

Article Title: A New York woman says co-op staff entered her apartment while she was out, took her dog and cat, and concealed where the dog went; three years later, an appeals court has let her trespass and distress
Article Text:
New York woman can pursue legal claims after co-op staff allegedly took her pets. (AI image)

Dog gets euthanised

'Apartment entry was emergency'

Appeals court allows two claims to continue

A New York woman who accused employees of her housing cooperative of entering her apartment without permission and taking away her dog and cat has won a legal battle to continue pursuing two of her claims. Nearly three years after the incident, a New York appeals court ruled on Wednesday, that Lisa Cinque could proceed with her claims of trespass and intentional infliction of emotional distress against Glen Oaks Village Owners, Inc, and its employees.Cinque alleged that the employees entered her apartment while she was away, removed her pets and later gave her misleading information about where her dog had been taken. She said she repeatedly tried to locate the animal but was unsuccessful. According to Justia , documents submitted during the case indicated that the dog had spent nearly two months at a shelter before being euthanised.On May 31, when Cinque, a shareholder in the cooperative housing corporation and a resident of one of its apartments, was away from home, two employees, Gina Catania and Justin Conklin, allegedly forced their way into the apartment without her consent. According to her, they searched through her belongings, took photographs, removed personal property, including her dog and cat, and left the apartment door open.The employees then gave her cat to a neighbour. Finding her dog, however, became a prolonged struggle. Cinque claimed that the defendants initially refused to tell her where the animal had been taken. When they eventually provided information, she said it led her to facilities that could not locate her pet.According to the court judgment, the defendants first told Cinque that her dog had been taken to "Animal Care and Control". She contacted several facilities but could not find it.Her lawyer subsequently demanded information about the animal's location. In response, the defendants said the dog had been taken to the Humane Society of New York. Cinque contacted that organisation as well, but it denied receiving her dog.She continued seeking answers, but the complaint alleged that the defendants refused to provide further information. Cinque accused them of deliberately making false statements that prevented her from discovering where her pet was being kept.The court records also revealed what the defendants submitted in their attempt to have the lawsuit dismissed. They produced veterinary records covering May to July 2023, which they said concerned Cinque's dog.Those records indicated that a dog had arrived at a shelter on May 31, 2023, and had been described to shelter employees as an abandoned animal without an owner. After remaining there for almost two months, the dog was euthanised on July 24, 2023.Cinque filed her lawsuit in September 2023, seeking damages for trespass, intentional infliction of emotional distress and prima facie tort.The defendants disputed the basis of her claims and asked the court to dismiss the complaint before filing an answer.They argued that a foul odour coming from Cinque's apartment had created an emergency that justified their entry. To support their position, they submitted the apartment's proprietary lease, the cooperative's house rules and what they described as body-camera footage of the incident.The lease and house rules allowed employees to enter an apartment in an emergency. The defendants maintained that the smell coming from Cinque's home met that condition.However, Cinque argued that the material submitted by the defendants did not conclusively disprove her allegations.On February 25, 2025, a court in Queens County refused to dismiss any of her claims. The defendants then appealed that decision, bringing the dispute before the Appellate Division, Second Department.In its November 4 ruling, the appeals court examined whether Cinque's allegations were sufficient for the lawsuit to proceed.On the trespass claim, the judges found that Cinque had alleged an unauthorised and forceful entry into her apartment. They also concluded that the defendants' evidence did not conclusively establish that the entry was legally justified. The court therefore allowed the trespass claim to continue.The judges reached a similar conclusion regarding the emotional distress claim. They considered Cinque's allegations that her pets had been removed, that information about her dog had repeatedly been withheld or misrepresented, and that the animal had eventually been euthanised after being taken to a shelter.The court found that these allegations were sufficient to support a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress at this stage of the proceedings.However, the judges dismissed Cinque's third claim, known as prima facie tort. They found that her complaint did not adequately establish the required allegations concerning the defendants' motivation or identify specific financial losses.The appeals court consequently modified the lower court's order, dismissing only the prima facie tort claim while allowing the other two claims to proceed. It also awarded costs to Cinque.
Article Summary: Appeals court allows two claims to continue against Glen Oaks Village Owners, Inc, and its employees. Lisa Cinque alleged that the employees entered her apartment while she was away, removed her pets and later gave her misleading information about where her dog had been taken. The defendants disputed the basis of her claims and asked the court to dismiss the complaint before filing an answer.

Article Title: Titanic's owners received $5 million within 30 days of the sinking; 114 years later, original insurance document resurfaces and could fetch $67,000 at auction
Article Text:
Just weeks before the Titanic disaster

Families waited years for compensation

How the 114-year-old document resurfaced

More than a century after the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic, an unusual piece of paperwork connected to the doomed liner's final voyage has resurfaced. An original insurance document linked to the ship's $5 million total-loss cover, arranged just weeks before the disaster, is set to go under the hammer in Britain, with an estimated price of up to $67,000. The document is being offered by British auction house Henry Aldridge and Son at its November 21 auction in Devizes, England. It carries an estimate of £30,000 to £50,000, equivalent to approximately $40,000 to $67,000.The document is particularly striking because it records insurance protection for a ship that was widely believed to be virtually unsinkable, yet disappeared beneath the Atlantic less than a month after the policy took effect. Its most remarkable detail, however, is what happened after the disaster: Titanic's owners received the full insurance payout within 30 days of the sinking, even as families of those who died faced a much longer wait for compensation.The insurance arrangement was taken out by the Oceanic Steam Navigation Company, the parent company of the White Star Line, which operated Titanic. According to the auction description and reports by PEOPLE, the ship was covered for a total loss of $5 million through an arrangement involving 77 insurers.One of the major participants was Atlantic Mutual Insurance Company, which covered $100,000 of the risk. The resurfaced document comes from Atlantic Mutual's archives and records its individual share of the wider insurance arrangement. It should not be confused with a single policy showing that Atlantic Mutual alone insured the entire ship for $5 million.The document was signed on March 27, 1912, with coverage taking effect on March 30 at 7 pm and continuing until March 30, 1913. It also contains a handwritten addition extending protection to Titanic's journey from Belfast to Southampton and the risk associated with its sea trials. The timing makes the document particularly significant. Titanic departed Southampton on April 10, 1912, on its maiden voyage to New York. Four days later, on the night of April 14, it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The ship sank in the early hours of April 15, killing approximately 1,500 people.The insurance settlement was completed far more quickly than many might expect following a disaster of such scale. Lloyd's, which had arranged more than £1 million in hull insurance for Titanic, confirms in its historical records that insurers paid the claims in full within 30 days. Lloyd's records show that the ship's hull alone was insured for £1 million. The risk was distributed among several companies and more than 50 Lloyd's syndicates, with individual participants taking different portions of the cover. The premium for the hull insurance was £7,500.The $5 million total-loss cover reported in connection with the resurfaced Atlantic Mutual document was part of the wider insurance arrangement. The auction house says the limits of Atlantic Mutual's policy were also paid within 30 days of the sinking.Auctioneer Andrew Aldridge told PEOPLE that it was extraordinary that the owners received their payout within a month of the disaster, when the funerals of many victims had barely taken place. He also described the words "total loss" in the document as particularly striking given how soon after the policy was issued the ship was destroyed.According to Aldridge, families who pursued negligence claims had to wait four years for compensation, eventually receiving a combined total of $663,000. His comparison highlights the difference between the insurance arrangements protecting the vessel's owners and the lengthy process faced by people seeking compensation for the human losses.Titanic carried 2,224 passengers and crew. It had only 20 lifeboats, with capacity for 1,178 people. Lloyd's historical account records that 1,514 people perished, making the sinking one of the deadliest peacetime maritime disasters.The ship's loss also became a major event in the history of marine insurance. Lloyd's records describe how news of the sinking initially arrived through wireless telegraphy, with conflicting reports circulating for days. Some newspapers even believed the ship had survived and was being towed to Halifax.The insurance document remained among the historical records of Atlantic Mutual, a US insurer founded in 1838. The company was eventually placed into liquidation in 2011 after suffering financial difficulties, including losses connected to claims arising from the September 11, 2001 attacks.Following its liquidation, historical material from its archives was included in an exhibition in New York. A dealer subsequently purchased the Titanic insurance document, according to the auction house and PEOPLE.Aldridge said the auction house had been unable to locate another surviving original insurance document relating to Titanic and described the item as unique to its knowledge. The estimate of up to £50,000 reflects its rarity and its connection to one of the most famous maritime disasters in history.The insurance document will not be the only Titanic-related artefact offered at the November 21 sale. Original shipbuilding plans used by Harland and Wolff, the Belfast company that constructed the liner, are also due to be auctioned.
Article Summary: Original insurance document linked to Titanic's $5 million total-loss cover is set to go under the hammer in Britain, with an estimated price of up to $67,000. It was signed on March 27, 1912, with coverage taking effect on March 30 at 7 pm and continuing until March 30, 1913. Titanic's owners received the full insurance payout within 30 days of the sinking. Families of those who died faced a much longer wait for compensation.

Article Title: ‘Blue Tsunami’ to ‘Dem-olition’: How the world covered US midterm election results

Democrats have swept to power in both chambers of the US Congress, delivering a crushing midterm blow to President Donald Trump and leaving Republicans facing a political reckoning halfway through his second term. The party scored historic victories in traditionally Republican strongholds, flipped key seats across the country and registered a series of firsts, including the election of the first Muslim senator and the first openly gay man to the Senate. The results have not only disrupted Trump's legislative agenda but also raised questions about the future of the MAGA movement and the road to 2028 Presidential elections.From a “Blue Tsunami” to a “Dem-olition” job, newspapers across the world found their own ways to capture the scale of the Republican rout. While some focused on the domestic political fallout and the growing cracks within Trump's camp, others highlighted the role of the Iran war and economic discontent in the Democratic sweep.The Times of India described the outcome as a political defeat for Trump, with the headline declaring that Democrats had stormed Republican strongholds, seized both chambers of Congress and won a majority of governorships.The Economic Times captured the scale of the Republican setback with a play on the colour associated with the Democratic Party. Its coverage highlighted how Trump's tariff policies and belligerence had come back to haunt his party, while examining the implications of the results for global markets and India's economic interests.The South China Morning Post went with a image of celebrating Democratic supporters and the headline “Blue Tsunami Sweeps the US”. Its subheading described the outcome as a disastrous night for Trump, with Democrats taking the House and Senate and leaving global leaders to reassess their strategies.The Financial Times called the results a crushing electoral rebuke to Trump. Its supporting headlines highlighted the role of the cost-of-living crisis in driving the Democratic wave, with voters sweeping Republicans out of power in Congress. It also pointed to the political blame game beginning within the Republican Party, with JD Vance pinning responsibility on the Iran war, alongside movements in oil prices and technology stocks.The French-language Canadian daily went for a short, punchy headline that needed little explanation. “Toute une claque” captured the scale of the setback for Trump.The Chicago Sun-Times brought wordplay to the front page with “Dem-olition”, combining the Democratic Party's name with the idea of a political demolition job. The cover featured Juliana Stratton celebrating with supporters after her Senate victory, placing a local electoral triumph within the broader national blue wave.Spanish newspaper El Mundo focused on Trump's response to the defeat, particularly his attempt to attribute the Republican losses to the war with Iran. Its front page featured the president against the backdrop of the US flag, with the headline highlighting how the conflict had become a factor in the electoral backlash.The Iranian newspaper described the result as an outcome fo the conflict between Washington and Tehran. The English-language daily, which is closely aligned with the Iranian government, portrayed the Democratic victory as a sign of declining American influence, with the headline “US Hegemony Crumbling; Iran Will Never Surrender”.The Daily Mail led with the headline: “MAGA Turns on Trump”, which was accompanied by a report highlighting how JD Vance and even Donald Trump Jr were blaming the president's handling of the Iran war for the Republican wipeout.The Guardian chose a play on the president's name for its front page, with “Trumped” appearing in large yellow lettering beneath a photograph of jubilant Democratic supporters. Its accompanying description noted that the president's party had been stripped of control of Congress.The New York Post described the Democratic victory as a "Blue Tsunami". Its front page featured an illustration inspired by Japanese artist Hokusai's famous Great Wave, with Trump appearing to be swept away by a gigantic blue wave.The Australian opted for a pun, declaring “The Donald Deflation” as Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress. Its coverage connected the Republican defeat to inflation, fuel prices and the Iran war, while examining the political damage to Trump's MAGA movement.The Washington Post took a direct approach, with the headline “Voters swing to Democrats” summarising the electoral shift. Its subheading said the party was poised to take power on Capitol Hill with an eagerness to thwart Trump's agenda.The New York Times described the results as a “forceful rebuke” of Trump, arguing that the Democratic sweep signalled the beginning of the twilight of his political era. It highlighted how voter anger over high fuel prices, the Iran war and allegations of profiteering had eroded Trump's support, even in traditionally Republican strongholds.The Wall Street Journal highlighted the historic victories in deep-red states, noting how the Democrats had flipped key seats and put control of the House beyond Republican reach. Its front page featured images of victorious candidates and celebrations across the country.
Article Summary: Democrats have swept to power in both chambers of the US Congress, delivering a crushing midterm blow to President Donald Trump. Newspapers across the world found their own ways to capture the scale of the Republican rout. While some focused on the domestic political fallout and the growing cracks within Trump's camp, others highlighted the role of the Iran war and economic discontent.

Article Title: US midterms: Trump's veto powers & how he can use them to block Democrats' agenda
Article Text:
Trump does not necessarily have to wait for a bill to reach his desk to exercise influence

How Trump's veto power works

Pocket veto: Trump's other weapon

Veto threats can shape legislation too

The Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections has dramatically reshaped the balance of power in Washington, handing the party sizeable majorities in both chambers of Congress and setting the stage for a confrontation with President Donald Trump. With Republicans suffering a stunning electoral setback, Democrats are preparing to push an ambitious legislative agenda, reverse some of Trump's policies and launch investigations into his administration.However, their electoral gains do not mean they will have a free hand in passing laws. Trump retains one of the most significant constitutional weapons available to a US president: the power to veto legislation. The president has already signalled that he is prepared to use it, posting a photograph of a red baseball cap bearing the word "VETO" on Truth Social as the scale of the Democratic victory became apparent.“It’s the power of veto. It’s one of the stronger powers that a president has,” Trump said after the rout.Trump has also warned that he does not want to spend the next two years blocking everything Congress sends his way."I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything," he told Politico. Nevertheless, with Democrats preparing to challenge his policies, the veto could become a central instrument in the political battle between the White House and Capitol Hill.The presidential veto is a constitutional safeguard designed to maintain a balance of power between the executive and legislative branches. Under Article I, Section 7 of the US Constitution, every bill passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate must be presented to the president before it can become law.The president has 10 days, excluding Sundays, to sign the legislation, return it unsigned with objections or allow it to become law. If Trump issues a regular veto, the bill goes back to the chamber where it originated, accompanied by his objections.Congress can still turn the legislation into law by overriding the veto, but this requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This is a significantly higher threshold than the simple majority generally required to pass legislation.Democrats' expanded majorities will give them considerable room to push bills through Congress, but they will remain short of the two-thirds support needed to override Trump's vetoes. Historically, Congress has overturned only a small proportion of presidential vetoes, making the power an effective legislative roadblock.Trump also has another option: the pocket veto. Under this provision, if the president does not sign a bill within the 10-day period and Congress adjourns during that time, the legislation automatically fails to become law.Unlike a regular veto, a pocket veto cannot be overridden by Congress. Lawmakers would instead have to reintroduce the legislation, pass it through both chambers and send it to the president again.This gives the White House another way to block legislation, particularly when Congress is approaching an adjournment.Trump does not necessarily have to wait for a bill to reach his desk to exercise influence. A presidential veto threat can pressure lawmakers into modifying legislation before it is passed.The White House can also communicate its position through Statements of Administration Policy (SAPs), which outline the administration's support or opposition to proposed legislation. These statements can include explicit warnings that the president intends to veto a bill.Meanwhile, Democrats have other ways to challenge Trump even without successfully passing legislation. They can use their congressional majorities to conduct investigations, summon administration officials, issue subpoenas and scrutinise government spending and policies.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has the power to veto legislation. The veto is a constitutional safeguard designed to maintain a balance of power between the executive and legislative branches. Every bill passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate must be presented to the president before it can become law.

Article Title: Trump Jr backs JD Vance's 'reason we lost is the Iran war' remark after US midterms defeat
Article Text:
Trump Jr endorsed Vance's lengthy post on X

Trump shifts blame after Republican losses

US President Donald Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, has backed Vice President JD Vance 's blunt assessment of the Republican Party's midterm defeat, throwing the spotlight on divisions within the president's own camp over the Iran war.Trump Jr endorsed Vance's lengthy post on X, in which the vice president blamed the Republicans' electoral setback on the administration's failure to address voters' concerns over the Iran conflict, rising living costs and US foreign policy."The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote.Barely an hour later, Trump Jr reposted the message, adding: "Every word of this is 💯💯💯."According to Vance, the four main concerns driving their discontent were ending the war, tackling inflation and the cost of living, putting America first and changing the country's relationship with Israel."If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance wrote.He also acknowledged that voters who had previously warned against the war were justified in their criticism, urging Republicans to use the election setback as an opportunity to reassess their approach.Trump, meanwhile, sought to distance himself from the Republican defeat, arguing that he was not personally on the ballot."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" he wrote on Truth Social shortly after polls closed on Tuesday.Democrats won control of both chambers. The Senate is projected to have 54 Democrats and independents who caucus with them, against 44 Republicans, with two races uncalled. They flipped at least seven Republican-held seats and more than two dozen House districts.
Article Summary: Donald Trump Jr has backed Vice President JD Vance's assessment of the Republican Party's midterm defeat. Vance blamed the defeat on voters' concerns over the Iran conflict, rising living costs and US foreign policy. Trump, meanwhile, sought to distance himself from the Republican defeat, arguing that he was not personally on the ballot.

Article Title: US midterm results: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as first Black woman governor, flips Georgia seat
Article Text:
File photo: Keisha Lance Bottoms

Bottoms focused campaign on economy and policy

Jackson's spending and attacks fail to prevent defeat

Georgia's political landscape faces a new test

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected governor of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman to hold the office after defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson in Tuesday's election, the Associated Press reported.Her victory also marks the first time a Democrat has won the state's gubernatorial race since 1998.A former mayor of Atlanta, Bottoms won despite a significant campaign spending disadvantage, with Jackson having spent more than $200 million of his personal fortune on his campaign. She will succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term.Bottoms' victory also marks a shift in a state where voters have historically been reluctant to elect candidates from Atlanta to the governor's office.According to news agency AP, the growth of Georgia's largest metropolitan area has been reshaping the state's political landscape.Although her election breaks a historic barrier, Bottoms largely focused her campaign on economic issues and her policy proposals rather than the significance of her candidacy.The descendant of enslaved Georgians, she has spoken about her family's history in the state and her grandfather's move from rural Georgia to Atlanta.“I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian,” she said. “I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville.”She also recalled how her grandfather had to “walk through these back doors” of downtown buildings that she would later enter through the front as Atlanta's mayor. She said her ancestry “is always present with me”.On policy, Bottoms called for expanding Medicaid to cover hundreds of thousands more people and raising Georgia's minimum wage to $15 an hour. She also pledged to increase pay for teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees.Her proposals included pausing new data centre developments, stopping the installation of additional automated Flock cameras used by law enforcement, and repealing Georgia's ban on abortions after the sixth week of pregnancy.“This is a life and death issue,” she said of the abortion restrictions, citing cases of women dying from miscarriages and pregnancy complications because doctors feared criminal prosecution under the law.Bottoms also pledged to “make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump”.During the campaign, she repeatedly contrasted her approach with Jackson's stated ambition to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and become the president's “favorite governor”.“I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” Bottoms said during the rivals' only debate. “I’m running to work on behalf of people like you.”Jackson, a businessman who founded Jackson Healthcare, entered the governor's race as a relatively unknown candidate but used his personal wealth and outsider appeal to secure the Republican nomination.He had defeated the sitting lieutenant governor, who had received Trump's early endorsement, as well as the state attorney general and secretary of state.During the general election campaign, Jackson attacked Bottoms' record as Atlanta mayor. His television advertisements featured footage of protests following the 2020 police killings of Rayshard Brooks in Atlanta and George Floyd in Minneapolis. He also criticised Bottoms for not seeking a second term as mayor, accusing her of abandoning the city.Bottoms, in turn, questioned Jackson's claims that he understood the economic difficulties faced by ordinary Georgians. She pointed to his company's government contracts and accused him of using money earned from taxpayers to try to “buy this election”.Bottoms' election comes as Georgia has increasingly become a two-party battleground. Democrats have won three US Senate elections in the state since Trump's first presidential victory a decade ago.The state also re-elected Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff on Tuesday. He will serve alongside Raphael Warnock, Georgia's first Black senator. Ossoff is also the state's first Jewish senator.Bottoms' victory follows three consecutive Georgia gubernatorial elections in which a Black woman led the Democratic ticket. Republican Kemp defeated Stacey Abrams in the previous two contests. Abrams, a prominent voting rights advocate and Democratic fundraiser, did not seek the nomination for a third run.Bottoms was among eight Black major-party nominees for governor on Tuesday's ballot. There have been only three Black governors elected in US history, all Democratic men.This year, Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth of Minnesota were both seeking to become the first Black women elected governor of their respective states.Republicans have controlled Georgia's governorship and both chambers of its General Assembly for more than two decades.Democrats were seeking to flip the state House in Tuesday's elections, while Republicans were expected to retain their Senate majority, leaving Bottoms potentially having to work with at least one Republican-controlled chamber.
Article Summary: Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson. She will succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term. It is the first time a Democrat has won the state's gubernatorial race since 1998. Bottoms largely focused her campaign on economic issues and her policy proposals.

Article Title: Immigration after the midterms: A new Congress, but who holds the power?
Article Text:
H-1B: One fee blocked, another proposed

Proposed increase in prevailing wages for H-1B and PERM positions

PERM: More scrutiny for employers and green card applicants

F-1 students: Is the US becoming a less attractive destination?

H-4 spouses: Uncertainty over work authorisation

What changes on January 3?

Democrats’ takeover of the House and Senate promises greater scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. But with the President’s executive powers intact and several major policy battles already before the courts, H-1B workers, Indian students and H-4 spouses may have to wait for relief.The Democratic Party’s victories in the US midterm elections have changed the balance of power in Washington, with the party securing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. But for millions of immigrants, international students and foreign professionals, particularly those on H-1B visas, the more important question is whether the change in Congress will translate into a change in immigration policy.The answer, according to immigration attorneys and policy experts, is far from straightforward.Democrats have secured at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate and, in the preliminary House tally, at least 231 seats against 141 for Republicans, with several races still being counted. The results give Democrats control of both chambers for the first time during President Donald Trump’s current term. The new Congress, the 120th, takes office on Jan 3, 2027.The change gives Democrats considerable powers of oversight and the ability to scrutinise the administration’s immigration policies. But it does not give them the power to automatically reverse executive orders, presidential proclamations or regulations already issued by federal agencies. That distinction is central to understanding what the election could mean for legal immigration.Cyrus Mehta, an immigration attorney, cautions against expecting an immediate change in direction. Notwithstanding the midterm results, he says, the President retains the authority to issue regulations and policies through executive action.“While there may be oversight committee investigations into ICE excesses and abuses, and DHS racial profiling, I think the administration will pretty much carry out its immigration agenda,” Mehta says.He believes the administration will continue to rely on executive powers, regulations and policy memoranda, particularly because passing major legislation in the Senate generally requires overcoming the 60-vote threshold.“Congress may be able to question the administration regarding the justification for the $100,000 H-1B fee for hiring workers from outside the US, but its authority is limited to just that: holding hearings and asking questions. The administration will continue to implement rules and policies,” he adds.Ashwin Sharma, a Jacksonville-based attorney, points out that a presidential proclamation can be revoked by the President who issued it or struck down by a court. A final regulation can be undone through new rulemaking or a Congressional Review Act resolution, although the President could veto such a resolution.Sharma adds, “What the new majorities actually hold is the power to deny appropriations to specific rules, the power to investigate and subpoena, and, in the Senate, the power to decline nominees and judges. Those are real, and they should take the most reckless anti-immigration tactics off the table. But they do not reverse the immigration agenda. Washington changed who holds the gavel, but not who holds the pen: for the next two years, immigration policy will be drafted in the West Wing and redlined in the federal courts. ”Rajiv S. Khanna, managing attorney at Immigration.com, offers a more detailed account of the tools available to the incoming Democratic majority. Congress, he says, can narrow the authority delegated to the executive through legislation, prohibit particular fees or write programmes such as OPT and H-4 employment authorisation into statute.But there is a significant obstacle: the presidential veto. A bill must be signed by the President to become law, unless Congress secures a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a veto.Khanna believes Democrats could instead use spending legislation to attach restrictions on funding for particular immigration policies. They can also use congressional oversight to demand documents and testimony from officials responsible for implementing controversial measures.The Congressional Review Act offers another possible route for challenging certain final agency regulations. It allows Congress to pass resolutions of disapproval through an expedited process, although such a resolution still faces the possibility of a presidential veto. Proposed regulations and presidential proclamations are not covered in the same way.Duden Freeman, a former senior official with the US Department of State (DOS), similarly cautions that a change in congressional control should not be confused with comprehensive immigration reform. “While the shift in Congress indicates increased accountability and oversight of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and DOS, I don’t expect most visa policies to change drastically,” she says.“Everything the administration does that is not in line with the Constitution is taken to the relevant courts anyway,” Freeman says. She adds that real immigration reform may be easier to pass with a Democratic Congress but harder to secure with Trump in the White House.For Doug Rand, a former senior official with DHS, the courts may prove to be the more consequential check on the administration’s immigration policies.“The most important check on Trump’s immigration actions may not be the new Congress, but rather the courts. The original $100K H-1B fee was already blocked by a federal judge, and similar attempts to restrict legal immigration will likely meet the same fate,” Rand says.The question, therefore, is not simply what Democrats can undo after January 3, but which of the administration’s policies can survive legal scrutiny.The H-1B programme is likely to remain among the most closely watched areas of immigration policy, particularly for Indian technology professionals and the employers who sponsor them.The Trump administration’s $100K payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions has encountered substantial legal resistance. A federal court in Massachusetts vacated the policy implementing the payment in June 2026, and the First Circuit declined to suspend that ruling in July. A second federal court in California blocked the fee in Sept. The administration has extended the underlying presidential proclamation through Sept 2027, but the fee remains blocked under the relevant court orders.However, a separate proposal could create another financial hurdle. DHS has proposed a $103K fee for certain cap-subject H-1B petitions through formal rulemaking. As of the date of this draft, it remains a proposal rather than an implemented fee.Kripa Upadhyay, an immigration attorney and partner at Buchalter, says: “While Congress could increase scrutiny and try to restrict the administration’s ability to collect the proposed H-1B fee by attaching a condition to government funding legislation, it cannot simply stop the separate regulatory process.”Snehal Batra, managing attorney at NPZ&B, makes a similar point, noting that the administration is pursuing many of its immigration priorities through executive action and agency rulemaking rather than legislation.“The President retains significant authority over immigration and can direct agencies like DHS, USCIS and ICE to pursue enforcement and regulatory priorities. While Democrats can increase oversight through hearings and investigations and make it more difficult to pass new restrictive legislation, they cannot simply undo existing executive actions. As a result, I expect the administration to continue advancing its immigration agenda through the executive branch, with many of the key battles playing out in the courts through challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act rather than in Congress,” she explains.Another concern is the proposed increase in prevailing wages for H-1B and employment-based green card programmes.Currently, wages are pegged to four levels at roughly the 17th, 34th, 50th and 67th percentiles of market wages. The Department of Labor (DOL) proposes to raise these thresholds significantly. Entry-level (Level I) wages could rise from the 17th percentile to the 34th percentile, aligning them with what is currently considered mid-level pay. The DOL estimates that the changes would increase the average certified wage by about $14,000 per year per position.Mitchell Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, offers an important political qualification. “While Democrats may resist certain fees and restrictions on foreign students, Wexler believes that increased wage minimums for H-1B and employment-based green cards, as well as broader authority for employer enforcement, could find support among some congressional Democrats. “Those aren’t one-party issues as a rule,” he says.Employment-based green card applicants could face another challenging period if the proposed changes to the PERM labour certification process move forward. The Department of Labour (DOL) is considering changes to recruitment requirements and additional protections for US workers, particularly in situations involving recent layoffs. The proposed overhaul had recently cleared White House review.There is also concern over the suspension of PERM processing involving eight major employers, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.The incoming Congress could demand explanations from the Department of Labor, according to the attorneys. Upadhyay says: “Congress can’t end the investigation. It can, however, demand the evidence behind it, question why only some companies were singled out, and probe the process. The most likely route to relief is a legal challenge by the companies themselves.”For international students, particularly those from India, two policy changes are of concern: the proposed elimination of Duration of Status and the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). The Duration of Status rule was finalised but blocked by a federal court before it could take effect. It would replace the existing framework with fixed periods of admission, subject to extensions.DHS has proposed charging $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent periods, including STEM OPT extensions. Universities would be required to pay the fee before recommending a student for OPT and could potentially pass the expense on to students or employers.On this front, Khanna believes that the House Oversight Committee is where a Democratic majority can make itself felt fastest. Under House rules, the committee may investigate any matter at any time, even one assigned to another committee. It can compel testimony and the production of documents by subpoena. Officials involved in the $100,000 fee, the OPT fee and the EAD backlog could therefore be called to testify under oath, while the internal analyses behind these measures could be demanded.Immigration attorneys also believe litigation could be the quickest way to challenge the proposed OPT fee.The automatic extension of Employment Authorisation Documents (EADs) has ended for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025. DHS subsequently issued a final rule making the change permanent.Khanna points out that Senate Democrats have already filed a resolution, S.J.Res. 99, against the interim version of this rule. However, the resolution would still require the President’s signature to take effect.The next concern is the possibility of eliminating the H-4 EAD programme altogether. Batra says: “Because the H-4 EAD has existed for more than a decade, DHS would be required to do more than simply change its mind. The agency would need to acknowledge its policy reversal, provide a reasoned basis for the change, and address the significant reliance interests of H-4 families and their employers. Given the program’s longevity and the economic impact of rescission, any attempt to eliminate H-4 work authorisation would likely face substantial legal and procedural hurdles. ”The incoming Democratic Congress will have more opportunities to scrutinise the administration’s immigration actions. Hearings, investigations, subpoenas and funding negotiations could put pressure on federal agencies.But the attorneys do not expect the new congressional majority to automatically reverse the administration’s immigration agenda.Upadhyay believes that, for the immediate future, the courts and the presidential veto will matter more than the congressional majority.“Where House oversight can do the most good is on pretextual delays. This administration has been assassinating legal immigration by slowing it to a crawl, without changing a single rule. Since Dec 2025, when the State Department ordered an online-presence review of every H-1B and H-4 applicant, consulates in India have cut daily interviews and cancelled appointments wholesale. Individuals are now offered H-1B interview dates more than six months out, and H-4 spouses often find no appointment at all. At USCIS, a standalone H-4 EAD renewal is taking more than a year, and with automatic extensions gone, every month of delay past the card’s expiry is a month a lawfully present spouse cannot work. None of these nefarious, underhanded schemes, too numerous to count, appears in the Federal Register. The Oversight Committee can demand the staffing figures, the internal guidance and the emails behind these slowdowns, and put the officials responsible under oath. Like noxious black mould, furtive toxicity withers in daylight; dispelling secrecy is an important antidote,” Khanna emphasises.The incoming Congress may be able to subject immigration policy to greater scrutiny and use funding negotiations to press the administration. But with executive authority intact and major disputes continuing in the courts, the practical impact on H-1B workers, students, H-4 spouses and employment-based green card applicants will depend largely on how those legal and regulatory battles unfold.
Article Summary: Democrats’ takeover of the House and Senate promises greater scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. But with the President's executive powers intact and several major policy battles already before the courts, H-1B workers, Indian students and H-4 spouses may have to wait for relief.

Article Title: In 2022, a 191-acre Indiana land listing triggered a much bigger conservation effort; 3,950 acres of former coal-mining land are now protected for wildlife and public access, a new account of the proj
Article Text:
How a small land deal became a 3,950-acre conservation project

Why protecting this landscape matters

A new public space for outdoor recreation

What began as an attempt to save a 191-acre piece of land from a potential sale has grown into one of southern Indiana's significant conservation efforts. Nearly 4,000 acres in Sullivan County are now permanently protected as the Busseron Creek Fish and Wildlife Area, preserving wetlands, forests and former coal-mining land for wildlife and public recreation. A November 2 account by the Conservation Law Center, alongside reports from Indiana Public Media and The Indianapolis Star, has shed more light on how an unexpected property listing in 2022 set the larger project in motion. The conservation effort began when the Conservation Law Center's Southern Indiana Sentinel Landscape team noticed a 191-acre parcel listed on the open market in late 2022. The property was part of a much larger holding of nearly 4,000 acres owned by American Land Holdings of Indiana, a subsidiary of Peabody Energy.The land had a complicated history. Much of it had previously been part of the Minnehaha Fish and Wildlife Area, which closed in 2016 after the former landowner declined to renew its lease. The landscape, which includes reclaimed surface-mining ground, had gradually developed into a mix of bottomland forests, marshes, wetlands and upland grasslands. Conservationists feared that selling individual parcels could divide the connected landscape, potentially affecting wildlife habitats and the wetlands that help manage floodwater and filter water naturally.The Conservation Law Center worked with the landowner and a local realtor to take the 191-acre parcel off the market while a longer-term solution was explored. The Conservation Fund stepped in with immediate financial support, purchasing the property with the intention of eventually transferring it into public ownership.That initial intervention created an opportunity to negotiate for the entire 3,950-acre holding rather than protecting just the smaller parcel. The Conservation Fund and the Southern Indiana Sentinel Landscape worked with American Land Holdings to secure the larger property, helping prevent the landscape from being divided into smaller privately owned plots.The project eventually brought together several organisations and public agencies. Funding support came from the US Navy through the Department of Defense's Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration programme, the US Fish and Wildlife Service's Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Program, The Nature Conservancy, the State of Indiana and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation through Walmart's Acres for America programme.After more than two years of negotiations and fundraising, the Indiana Department of Natural Resources completed the acquisition in December 2024. The 3,950 acres, valued at more than $12 million, were permanently protected and established as the Busseron Creek Fish and Wildlife Area. The acquisition was also reported by Indiana Public Media and The Indianapolis Star.The property's location makes it valuable for more than its size. It sits in a transition zone between the western tallgrass prairie and the central hardwood forest, supporting a range of habitats that are increasingly important for wildlife. Its wetlands help absorb excess rainwater, reduce flooding and filter water, while the wooded and grassland sections provide shelter and feeding grounds for different species. The area also supports wildlife such as deer, wild turkey and migratory waterfowl.There is another reason the conservation project attracted federal support. The property lies close to the US Navy's Lake Glendora Test Facility, which is part of Naval Weapons Support Center Crane. Protecting compatible land uses around military installations helps preserve the surrounding environment while ensuring that nearby development does not interfere with military operations. This is one of the central ideas behind the Southern Indiana Sentinel Landscape initiative.The property opened as Busseron Creek Fish and Wildlife Area in April 2025, giving residents and visitors access to land that had previously been unavailable to the public for several years. Managed by the Indiana DNR's Division of Fish and Wildlife, the 3,950-acre area now offers opportunities for hunting, fishing, wildlife watching, hiking, foraging, trapping and other outdoor activities. Visitors can also explore its waterways using small boats, canoes and kayaks, while birdwatchers can observe migratory waterfowl gathering around its wetlands.The area does not have established hiking trails, but visitors can use available roadways and game trails to explore the property. The project also highlights how conservation efforts can depend on quick decisions and partnerships between organisations that bring different resources to the table. What initially appeared to be a relatively small land purchase became an opportunity to protect an entire ecological landscape.For Indiana, the result is not simply another addition to its public land network. It is the preservation of a former mining landscape that has developed into an important natural habitat, while ensuring that its wetlands, wildlife and recreational opportunities remain available to future generations.
Article Summary: conservationists noticed a 191-acre parcel listed on the open market in late 2022. The property was part of a much larger holding of nearly 4,000 acres owned by American Land Holdings of Indiana, a subsidiary of Peabody Energy. Conservationists feared that selling individual parcels could divide the connected landscape, potentially affecting wildlife habitats and the wetlands that help manage floodwater. The Conservation Fund stepped in with immediate financial support, purchasing the property with the intention of eventually transferring it into public ownership.

Article Title: In 2023, American singer-songwriter Jimmy Buffett left an estimated $275 million trust for his family; three years later, his widow and longtime adviser are fighting over its control
Article Text:
PC: PBS

Legal battle over managing Jimmy Buffett's wealth after his death

Why Savannah Buffett wants her father's wishes honoured in estate battle

Savannah Buffett's $75 million inheritance dispute

Cameron and Delaney focus on protecting the trust's assets

Legal proceedings continue over control of Buffett's legacy

Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims, allegations or financial details mentioned in the report.

When music legend Jimmy Buffett died in September 2023, he left behind more than a catalogue of hit songs and a business empire built around the Margaritaville brand. As reported by PEOPLE, his reported $275 million trust was intended to provide for his wife of 46 years, Jane Slagsvol, and their three children. But nearly three years after his death, the arrangements he made have become the subject of a bitter legal dispute. Jane is seeking to remove longtime financial adviser Richard Mozenter as co-trustee, while Buffett's children have taken differing positions on who should manage their father's fortune.Buffett, best known for songs such as Margaritaville, built a career that extended well beyond music. His business interests included restaurants, hotels, merchandise and other ventures associated with the Margaritaville brand. By the time of his death at 76 in September 2023, his financial interests had grown into a substantial estate.Before his death, Buffett appointed his wife of 46 years, Jane Slagsvol, and longtime adviser Richard Mozenter to serve as co-trustees of his trust. Their responsibilities included overseeing its assets and ensuring that distributions were handled according to the arrangements he had established.Savannah Buffett, the eldest of the singer's three children, has taken a position that differs from her mother's.She opposes Jane's attempt to remove Mozenter and wants him to remain involved in managing the trust.Reportedly, at a February 12, 2026, hearing in Palm Beach, Savannah's lawyer, Jared Gelles, told the court that his client wanted her father's original decision to be respected. He argued that Mozenter was not someone brought into the family’s financial affairs shortly before Buffett's death, but an adviser with years of experience and a detailed understanding of the singer's business and personal arrangements.Gelles described Mozenter as one of the people who had been deeply involved in Buffett's world for a long time. His argument centred on the value of that institutional knowledge, particularly when dealing with a complicated collection of assets.Savannah's disagreement with her mother has also been linked to an earlier controversy involving the possibility of disinheritance.The issue surfaced in legal filings in August 2025, when lawyers representing Mozenter submitted screenshots of alleged text exchanges between Jane and Savannah. The messages appeared to suggest that Jane had threatened to remove her eldest daughter from the trust.In one exchange presented to the court, Jane allegedly referred to the $75 million that Savannah could potentially lose, suggesting that her financial interest should be a reason for her to behave more like her siblings. Another message reportedly included the words, "Say good bye to that 75mil".During an August 18, 2025, hearing, Jane's legal representatives rejected the suggestion that she had taken steps to disinherit her children. They also said she had no intention of doing so, while acknowledging that the trust's terms gave her the legal authority to make such a decision.Buffett's other two children, Cameron and Delaney, have approached the dispute from a different angle. Rather than openly supporting either Jane or Mozenter in the disagreement over the co-trustee position, they have concentrated on the financial condition of the trust and its ability to meet obligations over time.The siblings have retained separate legal representation from Savannah. Their lawyer, Peter Sachs, told the court in February that his clients wanted to ensure their mother received the financial support their father had intended. At the same time, they were concerned about preserving enough of the trust's value for the other beneficiaries.Sachs also raised a point about the nature of the estate. Although its reported value is around $275 million, he explained that the trust should not be treated as if the entire amount were readily available in cash.Their lawyer made clear that they were not taking sides in the personal and legal conflict between the two co-trustees. Their position is centred on the long-term administration of the estate rather than backing one individual over the other.The dispute has continued through several court proceedings since 2025. In a more recent development, Jane appealed an order connected to the February 12 hearing that allows Mozenter to use trust funds for reasonable legal fees and related expenses arising from the litigation.The decision is significant because it concerns the use of the very assets both sides are seeking to protect. As the legal disagreement continues, the costs of resolving it also become part of the financial questions surrounding the estate.For now, his three children have not presented a united position on how the trust should be administered. Savannah wants Mozenter to retain his role, while Cameron and Delaney are concentrating on financial stability without endorsing either side. All three, however, have expressed a desire to see their mother receive the support their father intended.
Article Summary: Jimmy Buffett died in September 2023, leaving behind a reported $275 million trust. His wife of 46 years, Jane Slagsvol, and longtime adviser Richard Mozenter are co-trustees of the trust. Savannah Buffett, the eldest of the singer's three children, has taken a position that differs from her mother's. She opposes Jane's attempt to remove Mozenter and wants him to remain involved in managing the trust's assets.

Article Title: Three siblings discover their late father had two children from a secret relationship; court awards £170,000 to two sons, while all five biological children become entitled to shares of his £461,000 e
Article Text:
How the family discovered their father's secret relationship

Why all five children were initially entitled to the inheritance

Court rejects claim that their mother knew about the affair

Why the court awarded £170,000 to the two brothers

How the £461,000 estate was divided

Three siblings were shocked to discover that their late father had fathered two children during a decades-long relationship he had kept secret from his wife and their family. The revelation came shortly before his death, leaving the five biological children facing an unexpected inheritance dispute over an estate worth approximately £461,000. As neither parent had made a will, the estate was initially set to be divided equally among all five children under England's intestacy rules. However, two of the three siblings challenged the arrangement, arguing that their father's estate included money inherited from their late mother, who had not known about his other relationship. A court subsequently awarded £170,000 to the two brothers based on their financial needs.The case involved Michael Gymer, who died in 2020 at the age of 83, just months after his wife, Julie, who was 81. The couple had three children together: Shelley, Gregory and Lee.Shortly before Michael's death, the three siblings discovered that their father had maintained a long relationship with another woman, Beverley Madden, and had two children with her: Charlotte and Joseph. The relationship had reportedly continued for decades, with Michael concealing the existence of his second family from Julie and their three children.Charlotte and Joseph were 32 and 29 respectively when the inheritance dispute came to light. The five half-siblings had not previously known about one another.Neither Michael nor Julie had made a will. Under the intestacy rules in England and Wales, Julie's estate passed to her surviving husband when she died. When Michael subsequently died without a will, his estate, including the assets he had inherited from Julie, was initially due to be divided equally among his five biological children.The estate was valued at approximately £461,000, meaning each child was initially set to receive around £92,350.Gregory and Lee challenged this arrangement. They argued that a substantial part of the money had originally belonged to their mother, who had accumulated her share through years of work. They said it was unfair for that money to pass indirectly to Charlotte and Joseph, who were not Julie's children and whom she had not known about.Charlotte and Joseph argued that Julie had known about their father's relationship with their mother and had accepted that they could inherit from him.However, the court rejected this argument, finding no convincing evidence that Julie knew about the affair or the existence of the two children. Beverley Madden had reportedly claimed that Julie knew about the relationship, but the judge was not persuaded by her account.The judge described all five children as innocent of their father's deception. The dispute, therefore, was not about whether Charlotte and Joseph were Michael's biological children or whether they were entitled to inherit from him. It centred on whether the original equal division adequately provided for Gregory and Lee, given the circumstances surrounding the money their father had inherited from Julie.Gregory and Lee brought their claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, which allows eligible people to ask a court to reconsider an estate's distribution if they believe reasonable financial provision has not been made for them.After considering the circumstances and the financial needs of the five children, the judge ordered that £170,000 be returned to Julie's estate and divided between Gregory and Lee. Their sister Shelley did not receive an additional award because the judge found that she did not have the same financial need.The decision meant that the two brothers received additional provision from the money associated with their late mother, while Charlotte and Joseph remained entitled to inherit from their father.Following the ruling, Gregory and Lee were each expected to receive approximately £143,000, including their additional awards of around £85,000. Their sister Shelley, along with their father's two children from the secret relationship, Charlotte and Joseph, were each expected to receive approximately £58,000. This meant all five children retained a share of Michael's estate, but Gregory and Lee received larger portions because of the court's additional provision for their financial needs. The figures were rounded, and The Times reported that the precise distribution was to be finalised in a subsequent court order.
Article Summary: Michael Gymer died in 2020 at the age of 83, just months after his wife, Julie, who was 81. The couple had three children together: Shelley, Gregory and Lee. When Michael died without a will, his estate, including the assets he had inherited from Julie, was initially due to be divided equally among his five biological children. Two of the three siblings challenged the arrangement. They argued that their father's estate included money inherited from their late mother, who had not known about his other relationship. A court subsequently awarded £170,000 to the two brothers based on their financial needs.

Article Title: A Massachusetts couple renovated a home gifted by the wife's parents using more than $1.5 million from his parents; after divorce, a court revived the dispute over who owed the money
Article Text:
Image: Canva

How a gifted property in Tyringham became a renovation project financed by the husband’s parents

Image: Canva

Default judgment against the husband and a lien on his share came without notice to his wife

A family court found the note created a sham obligation and made the husband solely responsible

Missing loan terms and unexplained repayment plans kept the question of a genuine loan alive

Renovations, a Viking stove and social status, the second dispute over what counts as a necessity

The ruling’s bottom line, if the loan fails against the wife, the lawsuit ends in her favour

A Massachusetts divorce, a renovated home and a disputed loan of more than $1.5 million came to a head on 11 August 2026, when the First Circuit Court of Appeals revived a fight between a divorced wife and her former in-laws. Her husband’s parents funded the renovation of a property gifted by her parents, then recorded the money as a loan. A family court awarded her the home after the couple’s divorce, yet a trust holding the parents’ claim sought a sheriff’s sale of her ex-husband’s share, and the appeals court ordered fresh findings on whether the debt was genuine.According to the First Circuit Court of Appeals ruling in the Cosel and Wendt case, also published in full by FindLaw, Molly Cosel and William Wendt, known as Will, married in 2014. Around the birth of their second child, Molly’s parents deeded a parcel in Tyringham, in western Massachusetts, to the couple as tenants by the entirety, a form of joint ownership for married partners. They planned to renovate one structure and build another, partly as a family home and partly as a studio for Will’s photography career. Will’s parents, Bill and Dalia Wendt, first paid through gifts. Those ran out by November 2017, and from February 2018 they supplied further money, which the court calls the Disputed Funds.The marriage began to deteriorate in 2019, and the loan paperwork followed. Will signed a promissory note. Molly did not. Until then, the money carried no interest rate or repayment timeline, though Bill, Dalia and the family accountant each said it was always a loan. Molly moved out temporarily and filed for divorce in February 2020.In November 2020, the parents sued Will alone in the Massachusetts Superior Court. He did not appear, speak to a lawyer or offer a defence, so the court entered a default judgment in December 2020.
