A writ of execution followed, and the sheriff’s department recorded it at the registry of deeds, creating a judgment lien. Molly was not a party to that suit.In July 2022, the Family Court’s divorce decree ordered Will to transfer his interest to Molly, required her to pay him $250,000, and made Will alone responsible for the note to the extent it was a legal obligation. The Massachusetts Appeals Court upheld the decree and noted that the Family Court was not plainly wrong to find the note created a sham obligation. The Family Court had also accepted that it could not rule on the parents’ rights under the note, so the decree did not cancel the default judgment.The parents then assigned that judgment to a 2022 family trust bearing the husband’s name, with the couple’s children as beneficiaries and another son, Geoffrey Wendt, as trustee. A sheriff’s sale of Will’s half interest was noticed for 16 September 2022. Molly sued on 19 August 2022 to stop it, and the Wendts, who lived in Indiana, moved the case to federal court. The district court granted her summary judgment, holding that the divorce wiped out the creditor’s interest and that the money was not spent on necessaries, a legal term for certain household expenses.The appeals court affirmed in part, reversed in part and vacated in part. It vacated the divorce ruling because the district court had predicted an unsettled question of Massachusetts law while facts that could make it unnecessary remained undecided. Molly, the judges held, was not a party to the default suit, so she was free to challenge the loan’s use against her property. A sham loan, or a scheme to burden a marital asset, could not be enforced against her.The facts pointed both ways. The money became a loan only after the parents learned of the marital trouble; Bill acknowledged that no terms existed before the note, and neither he nor Will could reasonably explain how Will, on a limited income, would repay the sum. The judges called the family’s legal manoeuvres “eyebrow-raising”. But Bill, Dalia and the accountant testified that it was always a loan, which left a dispute for the lower court to resolve.Massachusetts law makes both spouses liable for debts incurred for necessaries furnished to either spouse or their family. The term is not limited to food and clothing and, depending on social standing, could cover furniture and even a fur coat. The district court called the renovations high-end improvements, but the appeals court found three factual disputes.One was which work the Disputed Funds paid for: a driveway, a septic system, a Viking stove and a Sub-Zero refrigerator, with the timing unclear. Another was social status. Molly said she was a schoolteacher and Will an aspiring photographer, with a combined income below $180,000. Will described them as multimillionaires planning million-dollar renovations. The third was how to measure the spending against that standing.The judges rejected the trust’s argument that Molly’s move away meant the property was no longer her principal residence, finding that she intended to return. They also rejected Molly’s argument that the domestic relations exception, a rule limiting federal courts in certain family matters, barred the trust’s counterclaims, since neither the trust nor the Wendts were parties to the divorce.
Article Summary: A Massachusetts divorce, a renovated home and a disputed loan of more than $1.5 million came to a head on 11 August 2026. Her husband’s parents funded the renovation of a property gifted by her parents, then recorded the money as a loan.Default judgment against the husband and a lien on his share came without notice to his wife. A family court found the note created a sham obligation and made the husband solely responsible.

Article Title: A father excluded his four daughters from most of his £1 million estate after believing they were plotting against him; court finds delusions influenced his will and declares it invalid
Article Text:
How a father's relationship with his daughters deteriorated

Why he believed his daughters were plotting against him

The will that left his daughters with just 25% of his estate

What the High Court discovered about his mental condition

Why the court declared the will invalid

Why the court also examined the role of his sister and companion

Four daughters set to inherit under intestacy rules

A father who believed his four daughters were conspiring to have him hospitalised and take control of his property left them just 25% of his estate in a will made while suffering from delusions. Michael Gwilliam, from Gloucestershire, England, believed his daughters were plotting against him for financial gain and arranged his inheritance accordingly. When he died in February 2022, aged 79, his daughters discovered that most of his estate had been left to other relatives and people close to him. They challenged the document in court, arguing that their father's mental condition had affected his ability to make decisions about his inheritance. In January 2026, the High Court ruled that his delusions had influenced the will and declared it invalid, allowing his four daughters to inherit under intestacy rules.Michael Gwilliam had previously enjoyed a good relationship with his four daughters and his former wife, Christine. He lived at a farmhouse in the Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, and had consciously decided against making a will because he wanted his estate to pass to his daughters under the rules of intestacy.However, his behaviour began changing in late 2013. He became increasingly convinced that neighbours were deliberately harassing him, making noises around his property and attempting to force him to sell his farmhouse.His concerns gradually developed into a wider belief that people were conspiring against him. He began spending nights outdoors, watching his property and attempting to identify those he believed were responsible.The situation became serious enough for him to be detained under Section 2 of the Mental Health Act in February 2014 for assessment and treatment. Medical professionals identified persecutory delusions and hallucinations, but Gwilliam did not accept that he was mentally unwell.After his hospitalisation, Gwilliam began suspecting that his daughters, particularly Helen, were involved in a conspiracy against him.He believed they had deliberately arranged for him to be detained so they could take control of his finances and property. He also accused them of wanting to obtain power of attorney, sell his farmhouse and take possession of his belongings.His beliefs extended to accusations that his daughters had stolen his possessions and medication. He also thought they were attempting to have him declared incapable of managing his own affairs.The court later found that these beliefs had no factual foundation. His daughters had sought medical intervention because they were concerned about his deteriorating behaviour and wanted him to receive appropriate care.Medical records and evidence from people who knew him showed that his suspicions persisted despite repeated attempts to persuade him that he was mistaken.On December 3, 2014, Gwilliam signed his only will, changing the inheritance arrangements he had previously intended.Under the document, 75% of his residuary estate was divided equally between his sister, Sheila Gwilliam, his companion Joan Brooks and his nephews. His four daughters were collectively allocated the remaining 25%, meaning each would receive 6.25%.The will also contained a forfeiture provision intended to penalise beneficiaries who challenged its validity.The accompanying letter of wishes contained accusations against his daughters. It claimed they had conspired with their mother to have him detained and wanted to take control of his property and finances.According to the BBC, the estate was valued at between £750,000 and £1 million, making the disputed inheritance particularly significant for the family.The four daughters challenged the will, arguing that their father lacked the mental capacity required to make it because his decisions were influenced by fixed delusions.The case, Ginger & Others v Mickleburgh & Others, was heard by the High Court following a seven-day trial in August 2025.Judge HHJ Leslie Blohm KC examined extensive evidence, including medical records, police reports, correspondence, diary entries and testimony from family members and healthcare professionals.The court found that Gwilliam was suffering from late-onset schizophrenia associated with an organic disorder of the brain. His condition caused fixed beliefs that his neighbours were harassing him and that his daughters were conspiring to take his property.The judge noted that these beliefs continued even when family members and medical professionals attempted to explain that they were unfounded.The court also considered evidence of his increasingly disturbed behaviour, including spending nights outside his home, brandishing an air rifle and making threats against people he believed were responsible for the harassment.The judge concluded that his beliefs about his daughters were not ordinary suspicions or disagreements within a family. They were delusions that he could not be persuaded to abandon through rational discussion.The central legal issue was whether Gwilliam possessed testamentary capacity when he signed the document.The court applied the legal principles established in the 1870 case Banks v Goodfellow. Under this test, a person making a will must understand the nature and effect of the document, the extent of their property and the claims of people who might reasonably expect to benefit from their estate.A mental disorder does not automatically invalidate a will. However, a delusion that influences the distribution of an estate can undermine testamentary capacity.In Gwilliam's case, the judge found that his false belief that his daughters were conspiring against him prevented him from properly considering their claims to his estate.The judgment stated that had he not been suffering from those delusions, he would not have made the will at all. He would have continued with his earlier intention of allowing his daughters to inherit under intestacy rules.The judge therefore ruled that the December 2014 document was void for lack of testamentary capacity.The proceedings also examined whether Gwilliam's sister Sheila and companion Joan had influenced his views about his daughters.The daughters brought an alternative claim of fraudulent calumny, alleging that the two women had knowingly made false statements about them to turn their father against them and influence his inheritance decisions.The judge found that both women had made statements to Gwilliam that reinforced his suspicions and intended to induce him to make a will that was less favourable to his children.However, the fraudulent calumny claim was unsuccessful. The court was not satisfied that the women knew their statements were false or were reckless about their truth. It found that they genuinely believed the allegations they were making, even though those beliefs were unfounded.The distinction was important because proving fraudulent calumny required more than establishing that false statements had been made or that they had influenced the deceased.With the 2014 will declared invalid, Gwilliam was legally treated as having died without a valid will.This meant his estate would be distributed under England and Wales' intestacy rules, under which his four daughters were entitled to inherit as his next of kin.Speaking to the BBC after the ruling, one of the daughters, Ginger, described the outcome as an "unbelievable relief" after a long and difficult legal battle.She said the family felt vindicated and was pleased that their father's longstanding wishes had finally been upheld.The ruling also established that a person's apparent ability to discuss and sign a will does not necessarily mean they possess the legal capacity to make one. The court's decision centred on the effect of Gwilliam's delusions on his understanding of his daughters' claims when he decided how his estate should be distributed.
Article Summary: Michael Gwilliam, from Gloucestershire, believed his daughters were plotting against him and arranged his inheritance accordingly. When he died in February 2022, aged 79, his daughters discovered that most of his estate had been left to other relatives and people close to him. They challenged the document in court, arguing that their father's mental condition had affected his ability to make decisions about his inheritance. The High Court ruled that his delusions had influenced the will and declared it invalid, allowing his four daughters to inherit under intestacy rules.

Article Title: California man dances to Bee Gees' 'Stayin' Alive' at Halloween-themed 97th birthday party; dies hours later after an unforgettable final celebration
Article Text:
A Halloween-themed birthday celebration

The special cake made for Vito

His final dance to the Bee Gees' 'Stayin' Alive'

Vito's best friend confirms his death

Baker's tribute to the 97-year-old

Social media reacts to the unusual coincidence

A 97-year-old California man named Vito has gone viral after footage showed him dancing to the Bee Gees' iconic song 'Stayin' Alive' at his birthday party, just hours before his death later that same night. Vito had wanted to celebrate his 97th birthday with a Halloween-themed party, bringing together friends for an evening of music, cake and dancing. However, what began as a lively celebration took an unexpected turn when he died shortly after the guests sang Happy Birthday. Videos of the occasion, shared by Los Angeles-based baker Eden Malinoff, have since attracted widespread attention, with viewers struck by the extraordinary coincidence involving the song's title and the timing of his final moments.Vito wanted to mark his 97th birthday with what Malinoff described as a "Halloween-birthday rager". The baker, who runs Baked SoCal, shared that Vito was part of her wider friendship group, which included people in their 20s and 30s.Despite the age difference, she described him as someone who loved life and could keep up with his younger friends. Malinoff said he was the life of the party and had an energetic personality that made him stand out among the group.In her November 2 TikTok post, she shared footage of the preparations for the celebration, explaining that she wanted to make a special cake for the occasion. She also recalled how Vito had previously shared his secret to a long life: "Don't drink cheap."Malinoff prepared a red wine chocolate cake for the birthday celebration, drawing inspiration from Vito's fondness for good wine.The cake featured prominently in her video, which showed her preparing the dessert and sharing glimpses of the gathering. She also included footage of Vito enjoying the party, surrounded by friends and guests who had come together to celebrate his milestone birthday.The baker later described the occasion as a celebration of Vito's long and full life, saying she was grateful to have been part of it.One of the most widely shared moments from the celebration showed Vito dancing enthusiastically to 'Stayin' Alive', the Bee Gees' 1977 disco hit.In the footage, he can be seen smiling, clapping and moving to the music as other guests enjoy the party. The song's title has since become the central talking point surrounding the story because Vito died later that same night.Malinoff shared a longer version of the dance footage on November 3, confirming the song that was playing before his death. The video quickly attracted attention, with viewers reacting to the unexpected coincidence.Following the initial video, Vito's best friend shared an account of what happened that night. He confirmed that the 97-year-old died at the birthday celebration, shortly after the guests had sung Happy Birthday."He did pass away that night surrounded by his best friends just after we sang him happy birthday. He got a good dance in right before. It was an amazing birthday party," the friend wrote.He also revealed that Vito had been dealing with medical issues, although his friends had not realised how serious they were. According to the friend, Vito passed away peacefully with his favourite music playing.The message ended with a tribute to Vito and a thank-you to Malinoff for making the birthday cake.Malinoff described Vito's final celebration as a fitting farewell to someone who had lived life on his own terms."If there is any way that Vito could have chosen to go out, it would have been like this," she said in her video.She added that he had been surrounded by people he loved while they celebrated his long and full life. She also expressed gratitude for having been part of the occasion.Her post was captioned: "RIP to an absolute legend."The videos prompted a wave of reactions, with many viewers expressing disbelief at the timing of Vito's final dance and death.One user commented, "You can't introduce us to Vito and take him away in the same story!!!"Another wrote, "Wait, dying at your birthday bash is kinda fire."Some viewers also questioned how Malinoff could speak about the incident in a relatively light-hearted manner. Responding to the criticism, she explained that the way she remembered Vito reflected his personality and the life he had lived.
Article Summary: Vito wanted to celebrate his 97th birthday with a Halloween-themed party. Video shows him dancing to the Bee Gees' iconic song 'Stayin' Alive' He died shortly after the guests sang Happy Birthday. Videos of the occasion have attracted widespread attention.

Article Title: In 2015, Detroit's Claude P. Moore began building a ball from just two rubber bands; 11 years later, it weighed 11,578 pounds and broke a Guinness record, with volunteers using a crane to weigh the gi
Article Text:
Detroit's Claude P. MoorePhoto: Guinness World Records

It began with two bands

Eleven years of work

Breaking the previous record

Photo credit: Guinness World Records

A crane and a crowd

More than a record

What comes next

Sometimes, something you might start without much thought can become a brilliant work later on in life. And Detroit’s Claude P. Moore's experiment of building a ball from rubber bands is one such instance. In 2015, Detroit’s Claude P. Moore began winding together two rubber bands with no clear idea of how far the project would go. Eleven years later, that modest beginning had become an 11,578-pound rubber band ball, officially recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest ever made, according to Guinness World Records.The record was confirmed in August 2026 at Belle Isle in Detroit, Michigan, where a crane was used to weigh the enormous creation. Volunteers, family members and friends helped move the ball from its storage container and attach it to the crane, turning an unusual personal obsession into a public celebration of persistence. Read more details about it here:Moore’s connection to rubber bands began long before the record attempt. As a child living with hemophilia, a rare and severe blood disorder, he spent considerable time in hospital waiting rooms and doctors’ offices, where he would occupy himself by twisting workplace rubber bands into small balls. Those early moments became the seed of a much larger ambition. Moore later said that coworkers encouraged him to build a massive version of the childhood toy, prompting him to revisit an idea that had stayed with him since middle school.He had already made a rubber band ball “as large as a chair” during his school years, only for it to be stolen by a classmate. Rather than discouraging him, that loss appears to have left the idea firmly in his mind, eventually leading him to wonder whether he could create the biggest ball the world had ever seen.Building the ball was not a short-term project. Moore began in 2015 and continued adding rubber bands over more than a decade, eventually requiring a dedicated storage container after the creation outgrew his garage. The work demanded physical space, time and an extraordinary amount of patience. As the ball expanded, it became large enough to nearly touch the walls of the storage container, making it clear that the project had moved well beyond an ordinary hobby!Moore was not working entirely alone. He credited countless family members and friends, many of whom initially thought he was “crazy,” for helping him continue through the years of winding, storing and transporting the increasingly enormous object.The previous Guinness World Record for the largest rubber band ball stood at 9,032 pounds, or 4,097 kilograms, and was set by Joel Waul in Florida in 2008. Moore’s final creation surpassed that mark by a substantial margin.When officially weighed, Moore’s ball registered 11,578 pounds, equivalent to 5,251.69 kilograms. Guinness World Records described the weight as comparable to that of an elephant, a comparison that captures just how far the project had travelled from its two-band origin.The official ceremony took place at Belle Isle, where Guinness World Records adjudicator Chloe McCarthy oversaw the measurement process. Dozens of Moore’s friends, family members and coworkers attended, with many helping roll the ball out of its container and secure it to the crane.The logistics of weighing the ball were almost as remarkable as the record itself. Volunteers had to move the massive object from storage, attach it safely to a crane and transport it to Belle Isle for the formal verification.As the crane lifted the ball into the air, McCarthy entered the crane cab and confirmed the record-breaking weight. The crowd reportedly erupted in cheers, with shouts of “Alright, Claudey!” filling the park as Moore accepted his certificate.McCarthy later said that seeing the ball in person was very different from viewing photographs of it. She praised Moore’s dedication, effort and advocacy, noting that many people would have abandoned a project requiring 11 years of sustained commitment.For Moore, the achievement carries personal meaning beyond the number on the scale. He has documented his experience with hemophilia in his 2021 book, 'My Life with Hemophilia', and spoke about that journey during the record event.He also distributed signed copies of the book to people attending the ceremony, using the moment to raise awareness of the condition that shaped much of his early life. The rubber band ball became both a record-breaking object and a visible symbol of resilience.Moore’s approach to the project reflected the same mindset he applies to life’s challenges. “The only excuse for failure is the lack of effort,” he told Guinness World Records, a philosophy that clearly guided him through more than a decade of work.The record has given Moore a major milestone, but he sees it as only one step in a larger vision. According to Guinness World Records, he hopes to continue pursuing ambitious goals, including working towards ending world hunger.That ambition may seem a long way from two rubber bands in a Detroit garage, but the ball itself proves the value of starting small and continuing consistently. What began as a way to pass time in medical waiting rooms became a record recognised around the world.Moore’s story is ultimately about more than rubber bands, weight or a certificate. It is about turning a childhood habit into a long-term commitment, inviting a community into the process and showing that extraordinary results can grow from remarkably ordinary beginnings.
Article Summary: Detroit’s Claude P. Moore began winding together two rubber bands in 2015. Eleven years later, that modest beginning had become an 11,578-pound rubber band ball. The record was confirmed in August 2026 at Belle Isle in Detroit, Michigan.

Article Title: Tyreek Hill grew up in Pearson, Georgia; in 2023 his family foundation announced a $40,000 donation to the athletic programs at Coffee High and Atkinson County High, near home
Article Text:
Tyreek Hill’s family presented a $40,000 check to the athletic departments at Coffee High School and Atkinson County High School in May 2023. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Hill moved from Pearson to Coffee County for high school

The $40,000 check was presented during a free youth football camp in Douglas

Coffee High School in Douglas, Georgia. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The foundation has kept giving in Georgia since the camp

High school sports participation reached 8,266,244 students in 2024-25

Tyreek Hill was born in Pearson, Georgia and attended Coffee High School in Douglas, about a 20-minute drive away, according to WALB and the O’Colly. His family foundation presented a $40,000 check to the athletic department at Coffee High and Atkinson County High, as a post on the foundation’s website states. The Tyreek Hill Family Foundation announced the $40,000 donation on May 25, 2023. Athlon Sports revisited it in a report published on October 30, 2026 and Yahoo Sports carried a version of that piece.According to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, Hill was brought up in Pearson, Atkinson County, but went on to study at Coffee High from the time he was in the ninth grade. Hill told the paper that his grandparents felt he needed a change. O'Colly, Oklahoma State University’s student newspaper, described Atkinson County High as small and said his family chose Coffee High, known for its sports programmes and exposure. He studied there in football and track, then attended Junior College for two years.Hill, at that time, Miami Dolphins wide receiver, concluded a full-house camp on Sunday, May 21, 2023, with children of Coffee, Atkinson and Irwin counties being invited, Daily Coffee Press reported.The foundation post mentions a $40,000 check to support the athletic programmes at Coffee High School and Atkinson County High School.Separately, a photo shared by Daily Coffee Press shows Hill presenting a check to Atkinson County, which was accepted by the principal and assistant principal of Atkinson County Middle School. However, the available posts do not clarify whether this was a separate donation or part of the previously reported $40,000 contribution. The foundation describes its mission as empowering children.According to Every.org, the foundation is a youth development charity organisation which operates from Pearson and received nonprofit status in 2017. The foundation's first gala, in December 2021, raised over $177,000 for youth mental health programmes, according to its website. In October 2024, Hill’s foundation launched a Hurricane Helene relief campaign for Georgia and matched donations up to $20,000, Fox 5 Atlanta reported. It also provides Cheetah Scholars, a college scholarship program giving out 10 scholarships each year and increasing by $5,000 to the scholarship fund for every touchdown scored by Hill in the 2024-25 season.Hill’s gift went to the school athletic department at a time when families are spending more to play. The Aspen Institute’s State of Play 2025 report found that the average family spent $1016 on a child’s primary sport in 2024, 46% more than in 2019. The same report cites the National Survey of Children’s Health, run through the US Census Bureau, which found that 55.4% of children aged 6 to 17 played sports in 2023, up from 53.8% in 2022. As mentioned earlier, the report refers to the Sports & Fitness Industry Association, which says that there was a growth in the participation of children aged 6 to 17 in team sports by 6% within a year in 2024, whereas their participation regularly decreases among teenagers aged 13 to 17.
Article Summary: Tyreek Hill was born in Pearson, Georgia and attended Coffee High School in Douglas. His family foundation presented a $40,000 check to the athletic department at Coffee High and Atkinson County High. The check was presented during a free youth football camp in Douglas in May 2023.

Article Title: Between 1984 and 1989, Oregon recycled the old asphalt on about 672 km (420 miles) of country roads, and over 75 percent of those projects were later rated fair or better
Article Text:
Representative image of a milling machine grinding up worn asphalt on a quiet country road. Image Credits: ChatGPT

How the recycling actually works

A representative image of recycled asphalt being packed down with heavy rollers right where it was milled. Image Credits: ChatGPT

Why quiet country roads were a good match

What the ratings do and do not tell us

Few things test a driver's patience like a cracked, bumpy country road. In the 1980s, Oregon found a way to give these roads a second job. The Federal Highway Administration’s guide , ‘User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction,’ says that between 1984 and 1989 the state recycled the old asphalt on about 672 km (420 miles) of low-volume roads, the kind people call country roads. More than 75 percent of those projects were later graded fair or better. That's not a perfect score. Still, it shows how recycling worn pavement can be a good, workable option for roads with lighter traffic.The method is called cold in-place recycling. It may sound complicated, but it’s actually pretty simple. Instead of removing old pavement, the worn-out top layer is ground up on site. The federal guide states that this fix is used when the depth of the damage is about 4 to 6 inches (100 to 150 mm). The crushed asphalt is mixed with new asphalt in either liquid or foamed state without any heating. Then the mixture is placed back in place and compacted with heavy rollers. The work is done on-site, so there are no long truck trips to a far-away plant. After a couple of weeks of curing in favourable conditions, according to the federal guide, a hot mix overlay is added on top.In most cases in Oregon, however, as stated in a 1991 article, the recycling layer was sealed with a sand or chip seal coating.Oregon kept this work on lightly travelled roads. In their 1991 Transportation Research Record paper, authors Todd Scholz, R. Gary Hicks, David Rogge and Dale Allen explained that every Oregon project was partial depth recycling. These roads generally carried fewer than 2,000 vehicles per day. Projects were also completed on county roads and US Forest Service roads. The authors also reported construction costs of approximately $1.70 to $2.10 per square yard. A normal 2-inch asphalt overlay was about $2.75 to $4.00 per square yard. These figures reflect prices at the time. The method has been studied closely by the Oregon State Highway Division and Oregon State University since 1986. The authors concluded that it seemed to be a viable option for low-volume roads. The federal guide also said that taking old asphalt to a plant on small roads will likely cost more. This makes fixing the road in place all the more tempting.The fair or better rating is useful, but it does not always guarantee perfect roads. The federal guide was careful about this point. It says that the cold recycled mixes were not recommended for use as a wearing course, which means that it must be protected by an overlay. Choosing the right road is also quite important. A road with a failing base or subgrade cannot be fixed by simply recycling the surface. The guide noted that eight projects in Pennsylvania received good to satisfactory ratings if a double seal coat was applied over the recycled mix. It also explained that more performance information was needed on resistance to rutting, fatigue and durability. The administration guide further added that more study was also needed on how cold recycled mixes would perform on busier roads. Oregon’s story is not about some magic fix. It's about a practical tool that, when crews chose the right roads, got fair or better ratings on most projects. That's good news to anyone who has dodged potholes on a back road.
Article Summary: In the 1980s, Oregon found a way to give these roads a second job. The method is called cold in-place recycling. Instead of removing old pavement, the worn-out top layer is ground up on site. The crushed asphalt is mixed with new asphalt in either liquid or foamed state. Then the mixture is placed back in place and compacted with heavy rollers.

Article Title: In 1989, New York paved two test roads with ground-up tyre rubber; after 3 years, the state transport department judged neither project economical nor successful
Article Text:
Ground-up tyre rubber are mixed into asphalt as a way to recycle old tyres into roads (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

Why New York ran the test

Each test road was split into five sections, with 1, 2 or 3 percent rubber by weight, a branded additive and a standard control mix (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

What the early results showed

Other states had similar letdowns

What the story doesn't prove

Turning old tyres into roads sounds like a win-win situation. It would cut waste, and roads could last longer. New York tried that idea in 1989. The state paved two test roads with ground-up tyre rubber in the asphalt, according to a Federal Highway Administration guide on waste materials in pavement construction. Three years later, the state transportation department said neither project was economical nor successful.In 1987, state lawmakers instructed the transportation department to carry out a pilot project involving recycled tyre rubber on state roads. This is explained in the progress report of the New York State Department of Transportation covering the first three years after the roads were built. The project resulted in the construction of two experimental roads during the summer of 1989. Each road had five test sections. Each test section was 2,000 feet long. Three sections had 1%, 2%, or 3% rubber by weight of the mixture. One section used a branded additive with larger pieces of rubber. The other had a standard mix kept for comparison. Both roads used what engineers called the dry process. In this particular process, ground rubber replaces a part of the fine aggregate in the mixture. The federal guide notes the most common US version came from Sweden in the late 1960s.It was sold in the US under the trade name PlusRide. The New York mixtures were applied as an overlay about 1.5 inches thick on top of the concrete roads.The state didn't just pave the roads and walk away. The progress report covers the first three years of tests. Engineers recorded how the roads were behaving twice a year. They took note of the type and location of damage. They ran deflection tests, which measure how much a road flexes under heavy load. Lab tests provided additional data. The early results were not quite promising. The report states that the rubber pavements were not performing as well as the regular mixes. The federal guide agrees with the state's finding. After three years, the New York State Department of Transportation did not see either of the overlay projects as economical or successful.The guide also provides information about the results from other states. Minnesota adopted the dry process on at least two projects since 1979. The roads performed well. However, they didn’t produce sufficient benefits to justify the higher cost. In Texas, one district’s rubber mix performed poorly and required a chip seal covering within three months. Washington State started using the dry process in 1977. The seven PlusRide road sections from Washington State varied from excellent to immediate failure. Eight dry process projects in Ontario, Canada generally performed poorly in the short term. The guide states that the results have been a mixed bag, with early failures being observed. It says that roads in service for several years showed little gain over regular overlays.That is not to say that tyre rubber doesn’t belong on roads. Both New York projects tested only one technique, the dry process. Most of the crumb rubber data is from the wet process. That method mixes rubber into the asphalt itself. The dry-process projects above varied widely in performance across locations and climates, and the guide cites a lack of field data to evaluate the method’s performance. More carefully controlled test sections are needed in different climates to get further insight. The guide says such sections may need to be monitored for at least five years, and possibly as long as 30. Recycling a material isn’t the same as improving a road. A green road has to work in the real world, with real traffic and make sense from a cost perspective.
Article Summary: New York paved two test roads with ground-up tyre rubber in the asphalt in 1989. Three years later, the state transportation department said neither project was economical nor successful. Other states have had similar letdowns with the dry process. The most common US version came from Sweden in the late 1960s.

Article Title: SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband, Robert, plan to distribute more than 2 million shares to eligible American children, with the first allocation expected in December 2026
Article Text:
PC: NASA

Gwynne Shotwell's pledge of more than 2 million SpaceX shares

Trump Account eligibility for children aged 11 to 17 in low-income ZIP codes

Shotwell's additional contribution to benefit eligible Texas children

How the Trump Accounts fit into the arrangement

Government agencies and financial partners involved

What the pledge means for SpaceX stock and children's savings

SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband, Robert, are moving ahead with a pledge of more than 2 million shares in the space company for American children's investment accounts under President Donald Trump's federal programme. The first distributions are expected by the end of 2026, with children aged 11 to 17 in lower-income communities among the intended beneficiaries. In an announcement shared on 30 October, Shotwell outlined the eligibility criteria, including children living in ZIP code areas with median family incomes of $57,000 or less. The planned contribution will also extend to other groups, including children in foster care and military families stationed overseas.Shotwell's announcement concerns a gift made by her and her husband rather than a donation being presented as a corporate contribution from SpaceX itself. The couple's commitment involves more than two million shares in SpaceX, which are being moved into escrow ahead of their planned distribution through children's investment accounts. At the time, she indicated that she wanted to direct a significant portion of her SpaceX holdings towards children, with particular attention to families living in areas with lower incomes.The new details establish the broad eligibility criteria and provide December as the expected distribution period.According to Shotwell's announcement on X (Formerly Twitter), the first allocation is aimed at American children aged between 11 and 17 who live in ZIP code areas where median family income is $57,000 or below. The geographical approach means eligibility is assessed using income information associated with a residential area, rather than relying solely on an individual family's reported earnings.There is also provision for communities where the population is too small for the US census to publish a reliable median family income figure. Children in these locations are included in the initial eligibility group, avoiding a situation in which families in sparsely populated areas are automatically excluded because comparable census information is unavailable. The shares are expected to reach the relevant accounts in December, once the administrative and transfer arrangements have been completed.Shotwell also outlined a further contribution expected to be finalised in the weeks following her announcement. This stage is intended to extend support to children in military families stationed overseas and those living in foster care. The proposed eligibility threshold for these children is a family income of $90,000 or less, with the relevant ZIP codes located in counties close to the Shotwell family's home in Texas.This second stage introduces a different geographical and social emphasis. While the first allocation is primarily organised around lower-income communities across the country, the subsequent contribution includes specific provisions for children whose family circumstances or living arrangements might otherwise make participation more complicated.The announcement did not provide a final distribution schedule for this additional group.Trump Accounts are a US federal initiative designed to give children access to investment savings at an early age. Rather than functioning as ordinary bank savings accounts, they are intended to hold investments that can potentially grow over a longer period.The programme has attracted contributions and public attention from several prominent business figures. Its structure has also created opportunities for private donors to direct financial assets towards children's accounts, bringing company shares into discussions about how young people might build financial resources before adulthood.Shotwell acknowledged the organisations involved in preparing the contribution, including SpaceX, the US Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service. The Dell Foundation, Greater Horizons and Invest America were also among the organisations she thanked.Two legal firms, Morgan Lewis and Gibson Dunn, were credited for their work on the arrangements. Their involvement reflects the administrative and legal considerations associated with transferring a large block of company shares into accounts intended for individual beneficiaries.Shotwell also recognised Brad Gerstner and Michael Dell for their contributions to the wider effort.The contribution places SpaceX equity directly within a programme intended to give young Americans an early connection to investing. For recipients, the potential benefit will depend on the value of the shares over time, as well as the rules governing when and how the assets can be accessed.For now, the immediate focus is the December transfer. More than two million SpaceX shares are being prepared for distribution, with the first group centred on teenagers in lower-income and data-limited ZIP code areas. A second allocation is expected to bring military families overseas, children in foster care and additional Texas teenagers into the arrangement.
Article Summary: SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband, Robert, are moving ahead with a pledge of more than 2 million shares in the space company for American children's investment accounts. The first distributions are expected by the end of 2026, with children aged 11 to 17 in lower-income communities among the intended beneficiaries. The planned contribution will also extend to other groups, including children in foster care and military families stationed overseas.

Article Title: American singer Tony Bennett's daughters say they received only $245,000 each from his estate; they are accusing their brother of taking millions through commissions and trust transactions
Article Text:
PC: AP news

How did Danny Bennett allegedly misuse his father’s estate

What does the lawsuit allege about Tony’s Alzheimer’s and finances

What does the lawsuit allege about Tony Bennett’s belongings

How has Danny Bennett responded to his sisters’ allegations

The daughters of late American singer Tony Bennett say they received just $245,000 each from their father’s estate, accusing their brother, D’Andrea “Danny” Bennett, of taking millions through excessive commissions, financial deals and trust transactions. Antonia and Johanna Bennett allege that their brother used his control over their father’s finances to enrich himself before and after the singer’s death in 2023. In a lawsuit filed in New York, the sisters also question the sale of their father’s music catalogue and image rights shortly before his death. They are seeking damages and Danny’s removal as head of the family trust.According to the lawsuit, Danny Bennett exercised control over Tony Bennett’s financial affairs both before and after his death through several positions of authority. These included serving as his personal and professional manager, holding power of attorney, managing his company Benedetto Arts and acting as trustee of the family trust.The sisters allege that their brother breached his fiduciary duties through what the lawsuit describes as “self-interested and conflicted transactions, excessive and unearned commissions”. They also accuse him of arranging substantial loans and gifts for himself and his children.According to the filing, these transactions reduced the assets available for distribution under their father’s will.According to AP news, the lawsuit also alleges that Danny Bennett took advantage of his father’s diminished capacity in the later stages of his life due to Alzheimer’s disease. The sisters claim he arranged financial deals that generated millions of dollars for himself and his company.One of the transactions highlighted in the lawsuit involved the sale of Tony Bennett’s music catalogue, along with the rights to his name, likeness and image. The deal with brand development firm Iconoclast took place shortly before the singer’s death, according to the filing. The sisters allege that the transaction was among the arrangements through which their brother financially benefited.Antonia and Johanna say they have received a “single modest distribution” of $245,000 each from the estate. They argue that the amount is “nowhere close” to what they believe they are entitled to under their father’s will, which provides for his four children to share his assets equally. The lawsuit seeks damages, with the amount to be determined at trial.The latest legal action follows a lawsuit the sisters filed against their brother in June 2024, seeking an accounting of their father’s assets and raising concerns about how the estate had been managed. The new complaint goes further, accusing Danny Bennett of breaching his fiduciary responsibilities and seeking his removal as trustee of the family trust.The sisters have also accused their brother of disposing of belongings with significant sentimental value to them in what they describe as a malicious and retaliatory manner. The complaint says their attempts to obtain financial information through the earlier lawsuit were followed by disputes over access to their father’s possessions. Antonia Bennett also claimed that a piano her father had promised her was in terrible condition when the sisters were eventually allowed to tour his apartment. They alleged that they were denied access to much of the property.Danny Bennett has rejected the accusations through a spokesperson, describing the latest lawsuit as another attempt to misrepresent their father’s wishes. The statement said: “Danny has followed his father’s plans with integrity and care,” adding that the allegations against him were unsubstantiated.The spokesperson also maintained that Tony and Danny Bennett had a record of unprecedented success together and said Danny remained committed to preserving his father’s memory and legacy. Tony Bennett died in 2023 at the age of 96. He had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2016, although no specific cause of death was given.Tony Bennett was one of the most recognised interpreters of classic American songs, best known for recordings including I Left My Heart in San Francisco. During his career, he released more than 70 albums, won 19 Grammy Awards and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. The legal dispute between his daughters and brother concerns the management and distribution of the singer’s estate following his death.
Article Summary: Antonia and Johanna Bennett say they received just $245,000 each from their father’s estate. They accuse their brother, D’Andrea ‘Danny’ Bennett, of taking millions through excessive commissions, financial deals and trust transactions. Tony Bennett died in 2023 at the age of 96. He had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2016.

Article Title: Where Is Bashir Zeb Baloch? Mystery mounts after BLA announces leadership change
Article Text:
BLA announces Bashir Zeb Baloch’s exit as chief, while unverified reports swirl over his whereabouts and possible death (Image credit: X posts)

NEW DELHI: Mystery shrouds the status and whereabouts of Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) Commander-in-Chief Bashir Zeb Baloch, following an announcement by the rebel group on Tuesday that he was stepping down from his post. The announcement stood in contrast to claims circulating on pro-Pakistan military social media accounts that suggest an assassination attempt or his death.Rumours across pro-Pakistan Telegram channels, citing unnamed sources, speculated that Zeb was the target of a poisoning attempt by a close confidant in Kandahar and was subsequently rushed to a military hospital.Other accounts went further, claiming he was eliminated in a Pakistani military airstrike inside Afghanistan in September — a claim that remains independently unverified.Zeb had emerged as the primary face of the BLA's major offensive, Operation Herof. Visuals released during the operation depicting him riding a motorcycle without security cover had created significant ripples across security and intelligence circles.In an official statement issued by the BLA, the group clarified the context around Zeb's departure saying: "Following the decision of the Senior Command Council in accordance with the constitution of the organization, former Commander-in-Chief of the Baloch Liberation Army, Bashir Zeb Baloch, will no longer serve as the head of the organization.""Until the selection of a new Commander-in-Chief, all administrative, military, and policy-making powers have been officially entrusted to the Senior Command Council, the highest supreme body of the BLA, while military operations across all fronts will continue without interruption," the statement from BLA said.The rebel group saidnthat during the reorganization of the BLA in 2018, the ideological and structural founder of the BLA, Ustad Aslam Baloch, had brought an end to hereditary politics and lifelong leadership, establishing the organization on the foundations of merit, transparency, and institutional principles."He set the guiding principle that no matter how influential, prominent, or high-ranking a commander may be in this movement, no individual can remain Commander-in-Chief for life. To maintain this ideological and organizational continuity, a clear and consensus-based procedure was incorporated into the BLA constitution so that, if the need ever arose, an established and peaceful constitutional pathway for a smooth leadership transition would exist. ""In accordance with this principle, a joint meeting of the highest bodies of the BLA was held on October 16, during which constitutional and organizational matters were thoroughly reviewed. During the meeting, all commanders unanimously decided in favor of leadership transition to impart fresh momentum to the organization's activities," the statement said."Our operational activities across all fronts continue without interruption. The name of the new Commander-in-Chief will be announced soon at the conclusion of the next phases," the BLA said.
Article Summary: Mystery shrouds the status and whereabouts of Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) Commander-in-Chief Bashir Zeb Baloch. Zeb had emerged as the primary face of the BLA's major offensive, Operation Herof. Unverified reports suggest an assassination attempt or his death.

Article Title: Asim Munir flags growing Hindu-Jewish ties threat to Pakistan and Muslim world, reveals Iran
Article Text: Iran's senior security official Mohsen Rezaei has claimed that Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir warned of growing ties between Hindus and Jews, alleging that the emerging partnership posed a threat to Pakistan and the wider Muslim world.In an interview with Iranian state media, Rezaei said Munir raised concerns over growing India-Israel ties during a four-nation security meeting in Tehran on October 26. The meeting was attended by Munir, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Rezaei, who represented Iran.Rezaei also claimed that the leaders shared concerns that Israel could target other countries in the region after Iran."They spoke very strongly against Israel. Mr Khalid bin Salman said that after you (Iran), Israel would target Turkey, and then come after Saudi Arabia," Rezaei said during the interview."Mr Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkish intelligence, shared the same view. Mr Asim Munir also spoke about the threat posed by Israel and the emerging bond between Hindus and Jews against Muslims and even Pakistan. These remarks reflect their information and concerns about how Israel may act towards them in the future," he added.Munir has repeatedly invoked religious differences between Hindus and Muslims, describing the two communities as fundamentally distinct.Days before the Pakistan-backed Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025, Munir had spoken about the differences between Hindus and Muslims in their religion, customs, traditions, thoughts and ambitions. He had also invoked the Two-Nation Theory.While Rezaei's latest account of Munir's remarks remains unverified, the reported comments are consistent with the Pakistani army chief's earlier rhetoric.Meanwhile, India and Israel have steadily expanded cooperation across defence, intelligence, counterterrorism, trade, agriculture, water management and emerging technologies. The two countries elevated their relationship to a Special Strategic Partnership during PM Narendra Modi's visit to Israel in February 2026.Israel had also openly backed India's right to self-defence during Operation Sindoor against Pakistan in May 2025. Israeli Ambassador to India Reuven Azar had said that terrorists had nowhere to hide.In February this year, Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu proposed a "hexagon of alliances" involving India, Israel, Greece, Cyprus and other countries to counter what he described as radical Shia and Sunni axes.In October, Netanyahu again named India as a key partner in his plans to build alternative alliances. He also warned that Israel could face a hostile US administration after President Donald Trump leaves the White House.
Article Summary: Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir raised concerns over growing India-Israel ties during a four-nation security meeting in Tehran on October 26. Munir, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Rezaei, who represented Iran.

Article Title: 'America taking its place': Shehbaz's rival Fazlur Rehman accuses Asim Munir of sabotaging ties with China
Article Text: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Monday accused Pakistan army of derailing Chinese investments under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor ( CPEC ), alleging that the country's mineral wealth was being used to advance foreign interests and facilitate a shift towards United States.In a social media post on X, Rehman claimed that Pakistan had disappointed Beijing by halting CPEC-linked investments midway and warned that the loss of Chinese confidence could deter other countries from investing in Pakistan."You have disappointed China, you have halted their investment midway, and when China is disappointed, the rest of the world will not come to invest in your country either," he said.He alleged that the US was stepping in to fill the space left by China, claiming that American officials had acknowledged this to him."And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me," he said.Rehman clarified that he was not opposed to foreign investment in Pakistan's mineral sector, saying the country urgently needed international capital, development projects and economic opportunities."We do not disagree with the principle of investment from around the world here.Multinational companies come, they invest; America is not immune to this, Russia is not immune, China is not immune, Britain and France are not immune," he said."And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me, and our esteemed elders here have taken those beautiful, beautiful stones to their offices and presented them, and the ambassador they have here at the time has also said it in her interview," he added.The JUI-F chief also alleged that politicians backed by the military establishment prioritised their personal interests and the demands of their patrons over Pakistan's economic well-being."These Pakistani politicians - whose priorities I know - in all such matters, they first determine their own share, and only then do they think about the country," he said.Fazlur Rehman also questioned the imposition of governor's rule and the declaration of an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, alleging that the measures were linked to concerns over the region's mineral reserves."On what grounds? Terrorism? The provincial government is aligned with the narrative of terrorism; it is the federation that is not providing support for that narrative," he said.He further alleged that the focus on terrorism had subsequently disappeared from the debate, while discussions surrounding mineral reserves had also been dropped."As soon as governor's rule was imposed and as soon as the emergency was declared, the topic of terrorism simply vanished, and from their side, the discussion of mineral reserves was dropped," he said.His remarks come amid Pakistan's efforts to attract foreign investment into its mineral sector, particularly in resource-rich regions such as Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.CPEC, a flagship component of China's Belt and Road Initiative, includes infrastructure, energy and industrial development projects. The initiative has faced challenges over the years, including security threats, delays and concerns over the safety of Chinese personnel and investments.
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman accused Pakistan army of derailing Chinese investments under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor ( CPEC) He alleged that the country's mineral wealth was being used to advance foreign interests and facilitate a shift towards United States.

Article Title: Pakistan's confidence crisis: Government officials plan to move families abroad for secure future
Article Text:
Shehbaz Sharif-led Pakistan govt faces confidence crisis as officials plan to move families abroad.

Pakistan is facing questions over the confidence of its own governing establishment, with defence minister Khawaja Asif alleging that some officials holding important positions in the country are planning to settle abroad, including in Portugal and other Western nations.The reported plans have drawn attention to a wider contradiction for the nation grappled with the economic crisis.While the government expects citizens to remain patient amid the country's difficulties, some people within the administration are said to be looking at opportunities and a more secure future overseas for themselves and their families, reported Greek City Times.The issue goes beyond officials moving abroad after retirement as it also raises questions about whether their families are already preparing to build lives elsewhere through overseas education, residency and eventual settlement.If the children of officials study and settle abroad, their families could become less dependent on Pakistan's institutions, even as those officials continue to hold positions of authority at home.The issue of family members studying abroad is also covered in Pakistan's official disclosure requirements. The Establishment Division's asset declaration form asks government officials to provide details of their children's education, including whether they are studying in Pakistan or overseas.It also seeks information about relevant family assets and expenditure.These requirements do not establish how many officials have sent their children abroad or whether they intend to settle overseas. However, they show that such financial arrangements are considered relevant to official disclosure and scrutiny.The reported plans come against the backdrop of a wider migration trend involving Pakistan's educated and professional workforce.In October, overseas Pakistanis minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain told the National Assembly that more than 1.8 million highly educated and professional people had left Pakistan over the previous three years, Pakistan Today reported.The people who moved abroad included doctors, information technology professionals, engineers, academics and skilled workers from several other sectors. Their departure raises concerns about the country's ability to retain experienced professionals across essential industries.The figures cited by the minister underline the scale of the movement of skilled workers out of Pakistan at a time of unprecendented economic crisis.
Article Summary: Pakistan facing confidence crisis as officials plan to move families abroad. Defence minister Khawaja Asif alleges some officials are planning to settle abroad, including in Portugal and other Western nations. Issue goes beyond officials moving abroad after retirement as it also raises questions about whether their families are already preparing to build lives elsewhere.

Article Title: Pakistan gas crisis: Families return to firewood as LPG prices soar ahead of winter
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan's fuel crisis forces families back to firewood and coal

With natural gas available for barely six hours a day and LPG prices soaring, families in Pakistan’s Rawalpindi are returning to firewood, coal and kerosene to keep their kitchens running as winter approaches.According to a report by The Express Tribune, households are increasingly relying on cheaper alternatives such as discarded furniture wood and sawdust. Residents are also facing steep increases in the cost of LPG cylinders, with a new domestic cylinder selling for PKR13,500 (approx Rs 4644), compared with PKR10,000 (approx Rs 3440) earlier. Refill charges have risen from PKR3,000 (approx Rs 1032) to PKR5,000 (approx Rs 1720), while commercial cylinder refills have nearly doubled to PKR25,000 (approx Rs 8600).The cost of firewood and coal has also climbed. Dry firewood is selling for PKR1,500 (approx Rs 516) to PKR1,800 (approx Rs 619) per maund, while ordinary firewood costs PKR1,300 (approx 447) to PKR1,400 (approx Rs 482). Coal is priced between PKR800 (approx Rs 275) and PKR1,000 (approx Rs 344) per maund, depending on quality, and sawdust costs around PKR700 (approx Rs 240) per maund.Muhammad Faizan, a furniture factory owner, told The Express Tribune that waste wood previously dumped near Nullah Lai was now being collected by residents for cooking.Shehzad Manzoor Kiyani, divisional president of the All-Pakistan Clerks Association, said inflation and unreliable gas supplies had forced government employees to return to firewood and coal. He said households were spending PKR10,000 (approx Rs 3440) to PKR12,000 (approx Rs 4127) a month on LPG.The household crisis comes as Pakistan’s LPG supply faces further pressure. The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) has raised the official LPG price for November to PKR 294,075 (approx Rs 1,01,138) per tonne, from PKR 279,341 (approx Rs 96,084) in October. The price of an 11.8-kg domestic cylinder has consequently risen by PKR 173 (approx Rs 59) to PKR 3,470 (approx Rs 1,194), taking the official retail rate to PKR 294 (approx Rs 101) per kg.But LPG is reportedly selling for as much as PKR 630 (approx Rs 217) per kg in the open market, while company-operated franchises are charging up to PKR 400 (approx Rs 138) per kg. Ogra said the increase followed a 6.47% rise in Saudi Aramco’s contract price, despite a marginal 0.12% decline in the average dollar exchange rate.LPG Distributors Association of Pakistan chairman Irfan Khokhar said the situation was serious because of the closure of the Iran border. He claimed that at least 70% of Pakistan’s LPG was imported from Iran, with the remaining 30% produced locally, and urged the government to curb market manipulation.Meanwhile, the Pakistan LPG Marketers Association has threatened to shut down businesses from November 16 if the government sidelines the private sector under its proposed LPG policy. Association chairman Ali Haider said the government should retain the sector’s deregulated structure, arguing that the private sector played a major role in imports.Haider said that of around 1.3 million tonnes of LPG consumed, approximately 225,000 tonnes were imported from the Gulf, largely by private companies. In a letter to petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, the association said the draft policy sent to the prime minister had been prepared without private-sector input and called for complete deregulation of the LPG sector.The association also criticised the petroleum development levy of Rs4,669 per tonne on locally produced LPG under the 2016 policy. The levy was intended to help state-owned entities, including Pakistan State Oil, Parco and Sui Southern Gas Company, import LPG during winter and emergencies. Haider alleged that despite billions of rupees being collected through the levy, these entities had failed to import supplies during the current shortage.
Article Summary: Natural gas available for barely six hours a day in Rawalpindi. Families are increasingly relying on cheaper alternatives such as discarded furniture wood and sawdust. Residents are also facing steep increases in the cost of LPG cylinders, with a new domestic cylinder selling for PKR13,500 (approx Rs 4644)

Article Title: India should arm Afghan Taliban against Pakistan: Sushant Sareen
Article Text:
-

India should consider formally recognising the Taliban government in Afghanistan and providing it with military assistance to counter Pakistan, strategic affairs analyst Sushant Sareen has argued, calling for a rethink of New Delhi’s approach to its western neighbourhood.Speaking on Faultline with Ananya Dasgupta on Times Axis, Sareen said India should not allow international consensus to dictate its Afghanistan policy. He argued that if Pakistan was using military force to pressure the Taliban, India should consider helping the Afghan regime defend itself.“If the Afghan Taliban are going to be bullied by the Pakistanis… then maybe we should help them militarily,” Sareen said. “So that they can also hit back.”He went beyond making a general case for military assistance, suggesting that India consider supplying Afghanistan with anti-drone systems, drone technology and missile capabilities.“If you can give them some anti-drone systems to the Afghans, if you can give them maybe some drone technology, which will help them fight back, maybe give them some missile systems or, you know, long-range rocket systems,” Sareen said.“Why not? I think we should consider it so that at least the Pakistanis cannot, you know, bully somebody into submission,” he added, arguing that India needed to be more willing to take risks if it wanted to project power internationally.Sareen’s argument comes against the backdrop of growing tensions between Pakistan and the Taliban, once backed by Islamabad but now increasingly unwilling to follow its instructions. The conflict has exposed the limits of Pakistan’s long-standing effort to exercise strategic influence over Afghanistan.Sareen said India should also reconsider its refusal to formally recognise the Taliban government, which came to power in 2021. He argued that recognition need not mean approval of the regime’s ideology or policies.“Recognition does not mean endorsement,” he said, pointing out that countries maintain diplomatic relations with governments whose actions they do not necessarily agree with.According to Sareen, the Taliban are the de facto rulers of Afghanistan and India already has a degree of engagement with them. He questioned why New Delhi should continue to hold back from formal recognition simply because other countries have not changed their position.Sareen said New Delhi should make its own assessment of what serves Indian interests, rather than remain constrained by concerns about how other countries might react.“The world doesn't ask us for our opinions before they start doing things,” he said.Sareen believes Pakistan’s Afghan strategy has backfired. Islamabad once viewed the Taliban as a means of securing influence in Afghanistan, but the relationship has turned adversarial as the Taliban has asserted its own interests.Explaining the mistake in Pakistan’s calculations, Sareen said Islamabad had mistaken a temporary alliance with sections of the Afghan population for lasting control.“You can rent an Afghan, you can't buy him,” he said, adding that the Afghans acted in Pakistan’s interests only as long as it suited them. Once they gained greater agency, they began pursuing their own priorities.Pakistan accuses the Taliban of providing sanctuary to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), whose attacks have targeted the Pakistani state. The Taliban, in turn, has resisted pressure from Islamabad and accused Pakistan of backing groups opposed to its rule.Sareen also discussed Pakistan’s interest in the Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghan territory that could provide direct connectivity to Central Asia. He said Pakistan appeared to see control of the corridor as a way to gain strategic leverage over the Taliban, but warned that such a move could invite retaliation.For India, Sareen argued, the question is whether the deteriorating relationship between Pakistan and the Taliban creates an opportunity to protect its own strategic interests. He urged New Delhi to consider both diplomatic recognition and military assistance, while acknowledging that a more assertive role would carry risks.His proposal raises a difficult question for Indian policymakers: could a former Pakistani ally now become a strategic counterweight to Islamabad — and is New Delhi prepared to act on that possibility?
Article Summary: India should not allow international consensus to dictate its Afghanistan policy, says Sushant Sareen. He argues that if Pakistan was using military force to pressure the Taliban, India should consider helping the Afghan regime defend itself. He suggests that India consider supplying Afghanistan with anti-drone systems, drone technology and missile capabilities.

Article Title: ‘Koi sharam hoti hai': Pak lawmaker mocks Khawaja Asif after Munir’s Iran visit
Article Text:
Fazl then turned Asif’s own words against him, repeating a phrase the defence minister had previously used to taunt PTI

Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman took a jibe at Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif over Field Marshal Asim Munir’s participation in a high-level regional security meeting in Iran, questioning why the defence minister was absent from the talks.According to a report by Dawn, Fazl raised the issue during his address to the National Assembly on Wednesday, referring to a meeting in Tehran attended by Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, alongside senior officials from Iran, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.“A defence pact is taking shape in Iran, a meeting is under way (there), and the defence minister is sitting here,” Fazl said, drawing laughter and desk-thumping in the House. Pointing to Naqvi’s presence at the meeting, he asked: “The interior minister is required there as well?”Fazl then turned Asif’s own words against him, repeating a phrase the defence minister had previously used to taunt Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).“There is your respect and stature — koi sharam hoti hai, koi haya hoti hai (have some shame, show some modesty),” he said, breaking into laughter.Responding in the National Assembly on Thursday, Asif denied that a defence pact was being negotiated in Tehran. He said the discussions had nothing to do with Pakistan’s defence or any related matter and argued that Munir had assumed a role focused on maintaining peace and dialogue following last year’s military conflict with India.The meeting brought together Munir, Naqvi, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, alongside senior Iranian officials, to discuss regional security and cooperation.A joint statement issued after the talks said the participants had agreed to continue their dialogue to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, particularly on peace and security.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also called for greater regional unity, saying closer cooperation among Muslim nations would help address shared challenges and resist external pressure.
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman took a jibe at Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif over Field Marshal Asim Munir’s participation in a high-level regional security meeting in Iran.

Article Title: Pakistan gas bowser explodes after truck collision, killing 2 and damaging 6 vehicles
Article Text:
Photo for representative purpose only (File)

At least two people were killed and five others critically injured after a gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's southern Sindh province on Wednesday, police said.The accident occurred on the National Highway near Rohri Interchange in Sukkur district. Preliminary reports suggest the gas bowser, which was carrying fuel under pressure, collided at high speed with a heavy trailer.The impact damaged the bowser's tank, triggering a powerful explosion and a fire that spread to nearby vehicles, Xinhua News Agency reported.Police said the two people killed were the driver and cleaner of the gas bowser. Both died at the scene after being caught in the explosion.Rescue teams and emergency services rushed to the site after receiving reports of the blast. The five injured people, who suffered serious burns and other injuries, were taken to a nearby hospital in Sukkur for treatment. Several remained in critical condition, medical personnel said.The explosion and subsequent fire also damaged or destroyed six other vehicles, including two fuel tankers, three heavy cargo trailers and a commercial Mazda truck.Police temporarily halted traffic on the National Highway and cordoned off the area around Rohri Interchange to allow firefighters and rescue teams to operate safely.Authorities began clearing the burnt wreckage and launched an investigation to establish the exact circumstances of the collision.
Article Summary: Gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's southern Sindh province. Police said the two people killed were the driver and cleaner of the gas bowser. Five injured people, who suffered serious burns and other injuries, were taken to a nearby hospital in Sukkur.

Article Title: Pakistan's gas mess: LPG prices soar, imported LNG piles up and the debt bill keeps growing
Article Text:
Expensive cylinders, dwindling reserves: Inside Pakistan's deepening gas crisis

A supply shock ahead of winter

Pakistan faces shortages after Iran war disruption

First, understand the three fuels

Natural gas: Extracted from underground fields and delivered to homes, businesses and factories through pipelines. Pakistan's domestic production has been declining.

LNG: Natural gas cooled into liquid form for transport by ship. After arriving at a terminal, it is converted back into gas, known as regasified LNG or RLNG, and supplied through the network.

LPG: Liquefied petroleum gas, made up mainly of propane and butane. It is stored in cylinders and is especially important for households that do not have piped-gas connections.

Domestic gas is running out faster than new supplies are arriving

Pakistan's domestic gas production falls 20% in five years

The LNG paradox: Too little gas, then too much

A financial hole worth trillions

Pakistan's gas circular debt surges due to supply shortages

Why Pakistan's govt cannot simply raise prices

The crisis reaches far beyond the kitchen

Power sector, households, fertiliser and industry: Who consumes Pakistan's gas?

A domestic LPG cylinder that cost around PKR 4,500 in Pakistan's Balochistan province has shot up to nearly PKR 7,000. In some parts of the country, LPG prices have reached PKR 600 per kg, more than double the official rate. With supplies disrupted following the closure of key border crossings with Iran, households are struggling to find affordable cooking fuel. Some have even begun turning to wood and coal.But the shortage has exposed a much bigger problem. Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining, its dependence on expensive imports has grown, and debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. Yet, even as households struggle with shortages, the country has also been dealing with surplus imported LNG that it cannot easily use or sell.On October 21, 2026, Dawn reported that LPG prices had climbed to as much as PKR 600 per kg in hilly areas and PKR 500 per kg in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, even though the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) had fixed the official October rate at around PKR 279 per kg. The regulator's notified price for an 11.8kg domestic cylinder was PKR 3,296.23.The disruption has since intensified. Reuters reported on October 23 that the closure of the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings with Iran had halted LPG imports, leaving tankers stranded and worsening shortages.Traders said Pakistan imported about 7,000 metric tonnes of LPG a day from Iran. In Balochistan, the price of a 12kg cylinder had risen from around PKR 4,500 to PKR 7,000. Pakistan cited security and anti-smuggling concerns for the border closure, while Iran pointed to technical issues. The two sides were consulting on resuming trade.The pressure is also visible in Rawalpindi and Islamabad. Dawn reported on October 26 that households facing limited piped-gas supply and soaring LPG prices had begun turning to wood and coal for cooking. Residents reported receiving natural gas for only about six hours a day, while LPG was selling at around PKR 600 per kg.Part of the confusion around Pakistan's gas crisis comes from the fact that three different fuels are often discussed as though they are interchangeable.The distinction matters because a disruption in one supply chain does not automatically mean the same thing for the others.The fuels nevertheless compete for the same household energy budget. When piped gas is unavailable or supplied only for a few hours, families turn to LPG. When LPG becomes unaffordable, some shift to wood or coal. The result is that a supply shock in one part of the system can quickly affect everyday life.The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), a government-backed research institution, said domestic gas production fell from 3,597 million cubic feet per day in financial year 2020 to 2,890 million cubic feet per day in FY2025. That is a decline of nearly 20% in five years. PIDE attributed the fall to the depletion of mature fields and a failure of new discoveries to replace the lost output.The Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25 offers another snapshot of the pressure on the system. It recorded average gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet per day during July-March FY2025, including 798 million cubic feet per day of imported RLNG.
