Domestic gas remained crucial, but imported supplies were already filling a substantial part of the gap.This is not simply a matter of turning up production. Gas exploration requires investment, time and confidence that companies will be paid for what they produce. PIDE has argued that payment delays, distorted price signals and the financial troubles of state-owned gas utilities have weakened incentives for investment. It has also highlighted the damage caused when domestic production is curtailed to make room for imported LNG.Pakistan began importing LNG in 2015 as domestic production became insufficient. Its supply arrangements include long-term contracts with Qatar, one lasting 15 years and another 10 years, as well as an agreement with Italy's Eni. These contracts helped secure supplies, but they also reduced the government's flexibility when demand changed.The problem became particularly visible in 2025. According to the US-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), LNG consumption fell by 1.21 million tonnes that year. Rapid growth in rooftop solar power and weaker demand from the electricity grid contributed to a change in the country's energy requirements.Yet contracted LNG supplies could not be adjusted easily enough to reflect the fall in demand.That left Pakistan facing an unusual predicament: A country struggling with gas shortages could also have more imported LNG than it needed at particular times.With limited storage capacity, surplus LNG had to be diverted into the domestic network or otherwise managed. But imported gas costs more than much of Pakistan's domestically produced gas, while household tariffs have often been kept below the full cost of supply.Diverting expensive imported fuel to consumers at lower regulated rates can therefore create losses rather than solve the underlying financial problem.IEEFA estimated that Pakistan's gas-sector circular debt stood at around PKR 3.3 trillion in its March 2026 assessment. The think tank also said unaccounted-for gas losses, including theft and technical leakages, were estimated at around 11.7% of gas handled.On October 20, Business Recorder reported that federal energy minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had told the National Assembly that Pakistan's total gas-sector circular debt and outstanding payments to domestic gas and LNG suppliers stood at PKR 5.454 trillion as of June 30, 2026.Of this, circular debt accounted for PKR 3.631 trillion, while outstanding payments to gas suppliers amounted to another PKR 1.823 trillion. The minister said the circular debt included PKR 1.448 trillion in tariff differentials, PKR 131 billion in receivables from power companies, PKR 210 billion in sales and income tax receivables, and PKR 59 billion related to litigation.Circular debt builds up when money owed at one point in the supply chain is not paid on time, preventing the next entity from meeting its own obligations. In Pakistan's gas sector, the problem has been aggravated by tariff gaps, unpaid bills, delayed payments and the cost of imported fuel.The consequences extend beyond balance sheets. When gas utilities struggle to recover the cost of supply, their ability to pay producers and maintain infrastructure comes under pressure. Producers, in turn, have less incentive to invest in new fields. Consumers may face higher tariffs, restricted supply or both.The IMF's concerns have continued into 2026. Dawn reported on October 2 that the lender had urged Pakistan to speed up work on targeted gas subsidies and address the sector's rising circular debt. The report said discussions were under way on shifting support from subsidised tariffs towards direct assistance for eligible low-income households, although data and ownership-related problems made the transition difficult.Pakistan's government has tried to balance financial reform with relief for consumers. On January 6, 2026, the Press Information Department reported that petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had announced, on PM Shehbaz Sharif's directions, that gas prices would remain unchanged for six months.The minister also said the government had negotiated with Qatar to divert surplus LNG cargoes to international markets while respecting contractual obligations.But holding tariffs steady does not automatically eliminate the gap between what gas costs and what consumers pay. Nor does it address the separate problem of LPG prices in the open market, where supply disruptions can push prices well above the regulator's notified rate.The Shehbaz Sharif-led government has also considered replacing broad gas subsidies with a single fair price, while protecting vulnerable households through targeted assistance. On August 27, the detroleum division said petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had urged reforms, including steps to curb gas theft, reduce losses and improve revenue recovery at Sui Southern Gas Company.Pakistan's Economic Survey for 2024-25 recorded average daily gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet during July-March FY2025. The power sector accounted for 973 million cubic feet per day, while domestic consumers used 777 million and the fertiliser sector 764 million. General industry consumed another 536 million cubic feet per day.These figures show why gas allocation is such a difficult policy choice. A supply shortfall can affect household cooking and heating, but it can also disrupt electricity generation, fertiliser production and industrial operations.Fertiliser plants are particularly important because their output feeds directly into agriculture. If gas supply or prices disrupt production, the effects can spread through fertiliser availability, farming costs and food prices. Industries that depend on gas for heat, processing or captive power can also face higher costs, potentially weakening competitiveness and investment.Until those structural problems are addressed, temporary relief may ease one winter's hardship without preventing the next shortage. Pakistan's gas crisis is bigger than LPG prices because the cylinder is only where a much wider failure becomes visible.
Article Summary: Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining. The country's dependence on expensive imports has grown. Pakistan's debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. A supply shock in one part of the system can quickly affect everyday life. Gas exploration requires time and confidence that companies will be paid.

Article Title: Afghan returnees face police raids, arbitrary detention in Pakistan's KP after emergency: Report
Article Text:
Emergency in Imran Khan's bastion, fresh fears for Afghan returnees in Pakistan

Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan have reported a rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following the military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in the province, as news agency ANI cited TOLO News report.Returnees said daily life had become increasingly difficult, with Pakistani police frequently searching their homes and restricting their freedom of movement. Several deportees alleged that they were being detained on flimsy pretexts and that law enforcement personnel were demanding bribes in exchange for their release.Mohammad Rahman, an Afghan returnee, told TOLO News that his family had moved from Punjab to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan's tenure in search of better living conditions.However, he said the situation had deteriorated sharply after Islamabad declared an emergency and imposed governor's rule, leaving refugees afraid to step outside for fear of arbitrary arrest and extortion.Another deportee, Sohail Khan, said authorities were conducting raids on residential properties at night while targeting and intimidating refugees in local markets during the day to extract money. Displaced families also recounted being picked up from their workplaces and subjected to humiliating treatment before being deported.The reported crackdown comes as nearly 27,000 Afghan refugees have returned to Afghanistan through the Torkham border terminal over the past three months. Officials at the Omari Temporary Settlement near Torkham said administrative arrangements, including 12 dedicated support committees, remain in place to provide essential assistance and manage a possible increase in arrivals.Meanwhile, efforts to resettle returning Afghans are continuing. The Taliban-led ministry of urban development and housing said more than 74,000 residential plots had been distributed to returning families across 22 provinces.The ministry added that land had been allocated across 27 dedicated townships, with 37 master development plans formally approved to support the reintegration of returnees.The Munir-Sharif duo imposed a state of emergency and governor’s rule in Pakistan’s northwestern province, a stronghold of jailed former PM Imran Khan’s party, PTI.
Article Summary: Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan report rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion. Comes after military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Pakistan reopens Iran border after week-long halt to commercial traffic
Article Text:
Following a week-long closure due to security threats, Pakistan has reopened the Gabd-Rimdan border crossing with Iran.

Security concerns preceded reopening

Pakistan has resumed cross-border trade with Iran through a major border point in Balochistan after a seven-day shutdown disrupted cargo movement, left transporters stranded and raised concerns about LPG availability as winter approaches.Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. according to the news agency PTI.Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, head of the Gwadar chamber of commerce and industry, confirmed that the crossing, also called Gate 250, was operational again.Kalmati said trucks and other vehicles carrying commercial goods were now permitted to travel in both directions between Pakistan and Iran.Welcoming the reopening, he said it would offer relief to traders and transport operators who had been unable to move their cargo during the closure. The restoration of supplies could also help address Pakistan's LPG shortage and ease pressure on rising food and energy costs.The crossing was shut on October 17 by Pakistan's commerce ministry, which did not publicly disclose the reason for the suspension. However, security concerns were believed to have prompted the move.The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases during the colder months.The situation worsened on Thursday when unidentified gunmen attacked trucks parked near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing. Dozens of vehicles were reportedly set ablaze, while several others sustained damage.Local authorities reviewed the security situation before allowing trade to resume on Saturday. Additional security personnel have been deployed to safeguard commercial convoys travelling through the area.The reopening also follows a visit to Iran earlier this week by Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who held discussions with Iranian leaders on bilateral ties and regional developments.Pakistan and Iran share a 909-km frontier between Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan province and Pakistan's Balochistan province. The border crossings are vital channels for trade and the movement of goods between the neighbouring countries.
Article Summary: Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases.

Article Title: 'Islamabad arming Afghans to fight anti-Pakistani insurgents': Ex-US envoy sounds alarm
Article Text:
The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul

Former US envoy Zalmay Khalilzad has sounded the alarm over reports that Islamabad is recruiting Afghans to fight anti-Pakistan insurgents, warning that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further.“There have been many reports that Pakistan is arming Afghans to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. Now there are reports that the Pakistani military is recruiting Afghans to fight against anti-Pakistan insurgents. As things currently stand, relations between #Afghanistan and #Pakistan are likely to get much worse,” Khalilzad wrote.Pakistan's information ministry on Saturday rejected Khalilzad's allegations as “baseless and misleading”, accusing him of promoting a narrative in support of the Taliban government in Afghanistan.The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul, with repeated border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan adding to tensions this year.On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border. Pakistani security officials and state-run media said troops, backed by artillery, destroyed Taliban posts during hours of fighting in Kurram district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Pakistani officials also claimed that troops killed an unspecified number of Pakistani Taliban militants attempting to cross into Pakistan from eastern Afghanistan. Kabul did not immediately comment on the clashes.Pakistan has accused Afghanistan of providing sanctuary to leaders and fighters of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban. Kabul has denied the allegations. The continuing violence has further strained relations between the two countries.
Article Summary: Zalmay Khalilzad warns that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further. The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul. On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border.

Article Title: 'Pak defeated, cannot fight us': Baloch rebels launch fresh strike; several killed
Article Text:
The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces, alleging that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG) during its ongoing Operation Almas.In a press release issued by its spokesperson, Major Gwahram Baloch, the separatist group claimed that Pakistani forces had suffered significant human and material losses at multiple locations and were forced to retreat following clashes. The BLF, as cited by news agency ANI said that the operation was continuing on several fronts with “full intensity and success”.Videos purportedly showing the ongoing violence have also surfaced. In one clip, a woman is heard saying, “Pakistan is defeated now & and cannot fight us”, as gunfire continues in the background. Another video showed a woman firing what appeared to be an assault rifle.The BLF further claimed that its fighters had overrun the main camp of the Frontier Works Organization (FWO) and hoisted the organisation’s flag at Gwadar Zero Point, describing the development as evidence of its advances during the operation.The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station, seizing official weapons and military equipment. It alleged that a police official was killed during the confrontation.In a separate incident in Gubd, the BLF said its fighters attacked a convoy of Pakistani security forces, destroying an army vehicle and killing or injuring several personnel travelling in it. The group also claimed that its fighters had taken control of the police checkpoint at Gubd Cross.
Article Summary: The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces. The group alleges that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG)

Article Title: Pakistan's elite want out? Khawaja Asif flags bureaucrats' alleged exit plans to foreign shores
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan defence minister Khwaja Asif

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats, alleging that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country, according to a report by Pakistan's Express Tribune.In a post on X, Asif said Pakistan had capable and honest bureaucrats, but alleged that many officials had made Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other European countries their permanent homes over the past several years.He claimed some officers had prepared for their relocation under a deliberate plan while employed by the Pakistani government. Portugal, he said, had emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He added that he had raised the issue on social media a few months ago.Asif said the officers whose names had surfaced in connection with the matter had held important positions and remained close to successive governments. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled after collecting substantial sums of money from several influential bureaucrats.The minister did not identify the officials or provide details to substantiate the allegations. He said troubling accounts were circulating about the matter and questioned whether senior officials who had enjoyed the privileges and respect associated with public service had remained committed to Pakistan.“Does it rise above all doubt and suspicion, or are they merely in transit?” Asif asked, questioning whether such officials viewed Pakistan as their permanent home or merely a temporary stop before settling abroad.
Article Summary: Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats. He alleges that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country. Portugal has emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer killed in IED blast during Balochistan operation
Article Text:
Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists.

A Pakistan Army major was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during a security operation in Balochistan province, while security forces killed four terrorists in a separate operation, the military said on Monday.According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, security forces conducted operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Gwadar and Jattakabad in Kalat district on Sunday following reports of terrorist presence.During an operation in Jattakabad, the forces killed four terrorists and recovered “a large cache of arms and ammunition”, the Army said.In a separate action, security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district. During the operation, 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation.“Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area,” the Army said.The military added that security forces and law enforcement agencies remained committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing the four terrorists and expressed grief over the death of the officer.“Major Wajahat Waheed sacrificed his life for the protection of our beloved homeland; the nation is proud of its brave son,” the prime minister said.Sharif also extended condolences to the officer's family and prayed for the elevation of his rank.Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, with security forces continuing operations to contain the violence.A day earlier, security forces killed eight terrorists during operations in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts.(With inputs from PTI)
Article Summary: Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists. Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation. Security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district.

Article Title: US-designated LeT terrorist dies after mysteriously falling from building in Lahore
Article Text:
LeT terrorist Chaudhary Muhammed Sarwar.

NEW DELHI: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim, one of the founding members of the outfit, died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday.The incident reminded of a similar death that had occurred in 2016 when fake currency kingpin, Javed Khanani, had died after falling from an under construction building in Karachi.Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League. He was a close aide of both Hafiz Saeed and current deputy chief Saifullah Kasuri. Sarwar's son had also died in a road accident a few months ago.It was in 2016 tha Sarwar was designated a terrorist by the US justice department who termed himself as a senior LeT memeber in Lahore active since early 2000s, holding various leadership roles in the group. At the time, he was LeT’s emir for Lahore, a position he has held since at least January 2015."As the LeT emir of Lahore, Sarwar maintains relationships with LeT’s most senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, Sarwar worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, and in early 2013, Makki asked Sarwar for money to pay for his travel within Pakistan," the US justice department had said in its statement."Sarwar had been directly involved in LeT fundraising activities and used the formal financial system in Pakistan to raise and move funds on behalf of LeT. For example, in 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities for the purpose of soliciting donations for the group," it added.
Article Summary: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday. Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League.

Article Title: 50 years after Nepal banned cannabis, top court orders regulated cultivation
Article Text:
Nepal SC directs govt to frame rules within three months for regulated cannabis cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial use, while recreational use remains illegal

Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes, potentially opening the door to a legal cannabis industry in the Himalayan nation. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation.The verdict, delivered on May 18, 2025, remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed during the violent Gen Z protests. Its full text emerged only last week, bringing attention to a ban Nepal imposed under international pressure.The court criticised successive govts for failing to implement provisions of the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, which permits certain forms of regulated cultivation and medicinal use."The failure to do so amounts to a refusal or neglect by govt to discharge its legal obligations," the court observed. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal.Rajiv Kafle, a prominent cannabis legalisation campaigner, has long called for Nepal to replace prohibition with regulation."In fact, regulation is a better policy option," he told TOI, pointing to the economic opportunities that countries with legal cannabis industries had already begun exploiting.How the ban came aboutDuring the 1960s and early 1970s, Kathmandu's Freak Street became a major stop on the hippie trail, drawing Western backpackers and Americans avoiding Vietnam War conscription. Govt-licensed shops openly sold marijuana and hashish, but pressure mounted on Nepal as then US President Richard Nixon intensified the 'War on Drugs'.Nepal revoked cannabis trading licences in 1973.The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, later criminalised cultivation, sale and consumption, while retaining limited regulated exceptions that successive govts failed to implement. Several US states have since legalised recreational marijuana.
Article Summary: Nepal's Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal. The verdict remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed during the violent Gen Z protests.

Article Title: 50 years after Nepal banned cannabis, SC orders regulated cultivation within 3 months
Article Text:
Kathmandu's Freak Street in the 1960s. (File image)

TOI

Grass Roots: How ban came about

Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes, potentially opening the door to a legal cannabis industry in the Himalayan nation. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation.The verdict, delivered on May 18, 2025, remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed in an arson attack during the violent Gen Z protests on Sept 9, 2025. Its full text emerged only last week, bringing renewed attention to a ban Nepal imposed in 1976 under international pressure, particularly from the US.The court criticised successive govts for failing to implement provisions of the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, which permits certain forms of regulated cultivation and medicinal use. "The failure to do so amounts to a refusal or neglect by govt to discharge its legal obligations," the court observed. It directed authorities to frame rules for licensing and monitoring the cultivation, processing, storage, sale, distribution, import and export of cannabis within three months of receiving the order."It is therefore the duty of state authorities to formulate such rules without delay," the judgment said in a published English translation. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal, and left any wider relaxation of cannabis laws to parliament.The ruling could bring new opportunities for farmers in Nepal's mountainous regions, where cannabis grows naturally and cultivation has continued illegally despite the ban. Campaigners have argued for years that prohibition did little to stop production while denying farmers a source of income. They believe a regulated industry could give growers access to legal markets and create jobs in processing, medicine and other cannabis-based products.Rajiv Kafle, a prominent cannabis legalisation campaigner, has long called for Nepal to replace prohibition with regulation. "In fact, regulation is a better policy option," he told, pointing to the economic opportunities that countries with legal cannabis industries had already begun exploiting.Former health minister Birodh Khatiwada, another advocate of legalisation, has questioned why Nepal continued to criminalise a crop that several other countries had begun permitting. "It is not justifiable that a poor country like ours has to treat cannabis as a drug," he said earlier, criticising the difference between restrictions in developing countries and changing policies in wealthier nations.Saurav Dhakal of Green Growth Nepal has also argued that cannabis cultivation could help rural communities, but warned that large companies should not be allowed to corner the benefits. "We need to make sure that legalising cannabis benefits the neediest Nepalis," he said, calling for small farmers and cooperatives to have a meaningful share in any future legal industry.Nepal has made several attempts to ease its cannabis restrictions, but little has changed on the ground. A parliamentary Bill introduced in 2020 failed to make progress, while a 2024 govt announcement allowing medicinal cannabis cultivation produced few results. Gandaki Province passed legislation in July 2026 permitting regulated cultivation for medicinal and industrial purposes, but federal restrictions continued to complicate its implementation.During the 1960s and early 1970s, Kathmandu's Freak Street became a prominent stop on the hippie trail, attracting Western backpackers, counterculture travellers and Americans seeking to avoid conscription during the Vietnam War. Govt-licensed shops openly sold marijuana and hashish. As then US President Richard Nixon intensified the 'War on Drugs', Nepal faced mounting pressure to shut down the trade.In 1973, Nepal revoked cannabis trading licences, closing the licensed hashish shops. The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, subsequently criminalised cultivation, sale and consumption, although it retained limited exceptions for regulated activities that successive govts failed to implement.Ironically, several US states have legalised recreational marijuana years ago, while Nepal continues to criminalise unauthorised cultivation and consumption.
Article Summary: Nepal's Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal.
